activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: Before DNA can be copied, the enzyme helicase unwinds the double helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds that hold the base pairs together.
story:
The pigs had knocked over the water trough again, and Eric was hauling the hose across the barnyard with his biology notes folded into his back pocket, when Anika's car came up the lane. She got out holding her own notes, rolled and beaten soft at the edges, and said nothing about the pigs. She just said, "I still don't have it."

"You don't have what?"

"Any of it. Transcription, translation. Mr. Kelly talks like we already know what a ribosome is." She came and stood at the trough while he filled it, and the pigs jostled each other to drink, their snouts making the water slap against the tin.

Eric's exam was Monday. His father had agreed to let him study out here instead of driving into town, on the condition that he check the far pasture before dark, and Eric had agreed because the barn was quiet in a way his bedroom never was. He had spent two days with the textbook, drawing diagrams on the whiteboard he'd carried out from the shop, and the more he drew, the more he suspected he was copying rather than understanding. He could recite the steps. He could not have explained them to someone who hadn't read the chapter.

"Say the part you know," he said.

"There's DNA. There's RNA. There's protein. The middle part is where I lose it."

He turned off the hose. "Okay. Watch this." He reached for the zipper of his jacket, which was half unzipped from the wind, and pulled it down slowly so the two sides separated all the way to the hem. "Before DNA can be copied, this enzyme, helicase, unwinds the double helix. It breaks the hydrogen bonds that hold the base pairs together. Like that. Like unzipping."

Anika looked at the jacket, then at him. "That's it? That's the whole first step?"

"That's the whole first step. It has to open before anything else can happen."

Tyler arrived at four, on the four-wheeler, having heard from Anika that there was a study session. He was the sort of student who memorized definitions the night before and scored better than he deserved to, and he sat on an overturned bucket eating sunflower seeds while Eric stood at the whiteboard. Eric drew the opened helix, then the RNA strand assembling along one side, and he called it transcription, copying the message into a form that could travel. Then he drew the message arriving at the ribosome, where amino acids were matched three letters at a time, and he called that translation, the message turned into a working thing, a protein.

"You made that up," Tyler said. "It's not like a message."

"It is like a message. It's exactly like a message. Somebody writes a note you can't move, so you copy it onto something you can carry, and then somebody reads the copy out loud and builds what it says."

Tyler spat a shell into the dirt. "That's grandiose. It's a molecule, not a post office."

But Eric could see it wasn't grandiose, or no more than anything was. He had spent the morning mending the fence line where the heifers had pushed through, and he had found himself thinking that the wire was DNA and the staple he pulled was the enzyme, and he had stopped himself because the analogies were multiplying faster than the facts. That was the risk. The jacket gave you the opening. It did not give you the rest. He knew the sequence of bases mattered, knew the copying had direction and rules, and he knew he could not yet say precisely why one strand served as the template and not the other, or how the cell knew when to stop. The exam would want those answers. He wrote at the bottom of his notes, in small print, "still fuzzy: termination, and why this strand."

They walked out to the far pasture as the light went low, because Eric had promised. The pond at the bottom of the field was edged with ice thin enough to see water moving under it. Anika crouched and put her fingers on the ice, and Tyler picked up a stone, and Eric heard himself saying, "Don't destabilize it," which was a word from his chemistry chapter, and Anika laughed at him for it.

"See, you do know things," she said.

They stood there a while. The heifers came to the far gate and watched them without moving. Anika unzipped her own jacket against the cold and then, catching herself, held the two sides apart with her hands, looking at the gap between them. "One strand," she said. "And the other one. So the copy gets made against one side, and the other side just sits there."

"That's what I can't fully answer," Eric said. "Both are there. I know what happens. I don't have all the why yet."

Tyler skipped his stone across the ice and it stopped a third of the way out, sitting black against the white.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: The Mishnah, the first major written collection of Jewish oral law, was compiled around 200 CE under Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi.
story:
The problem started in Ms. Chanthavong's classroom on Tuesday, when she assigned the debate: does the biblical prohibition on work on the Sabbath still make sense now, argued only from the text itself. Daniel drew the affirmative side, which annoyed him, because he didn't believe it. Marius had the negative and was already smug about it. "You're going to quote Exodus at me," Marius said in the hallway, "and I'm going to ask you what counts as work, and you're going to stand there like a lamp." Daniel said he'd figure it out. He didn't have a plan, but he had his uncle's house, where he went every Thursday anyway, because his mother had decided the family should habituate itself to Shabbat dinner again after his grandfather died, and somebody had to carry the dishes.

His uncle was a taciturn man who repaired clocks for a living and kept his books in the front room behind the register. That Thursday Daniel ate his soup fast and said, "I need to know where the definition of work comes from. The Torah just says don't do any work. It doesn't list anything." His uncle looked at him over the rim of his glass for a long moment, then wiped his hands on his trousers and stood up. From a shelf between two brass movements he took down a thick volume with a cracked spine, set it on the counter, and turned the pages until he reached the one he wanted, in Tractate Shabbat, where the thirty-nine categories stood in their ordered rows. He tapped the page twice and went back to his soup.

"Whose is this?" Daniel asked. "Who wrote it?"

"The Mishnah," his uncle said. "Compiled around 200 CE, under Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi." He said it the way he said the price of a watch battery, flat and certain, and then he was quiet again, which was how Daniel knew it was all he was getting. Daniel read for two hours under the lamp by the register while his uncle worked on a carriage clock and said nothing. He learned that the rabbis had taken a sentence, one sentence in a book of sentences, and built a whole architecture of meaning out of it, and that the architecture was not in the sentence itself, and also that it kind of was, because the categories were all things you did to build the Tabernacle, which the Torah connected to the Sabbath in the same breath.

He called Sandrine from the hallway by the coat rack, because she was on his team and because she was the only person he knew who read footnotes for pleasure. "Okay," he said, "so my whole plan changed. Marius is going to say the rule is impossible because nobody can know what work means. And I'm going to say that's exactly the reason it survives. The text was never meant to be a list. It was meant to be argued with. That's what the Mishnah is. It's not a clarification, it's a two-hundred-year argument that they finally wrote down." Sandrine was quiet on the line, then said, "That's not what you said on Tuesday. Tuesday you said the rule was obsolete." Daniel admitted that it was. "So you changed your mind," she said. "In a debate. That's supposed to happen after, not before." He laughed, and she laughed, and they divided the work between them.

The debate was Monday, in Ms. Chanthavong's room, fifth period. Marius came in with a prepared speech about electric lights and hospital shifts and how an ancient agricultural rule could not bind a society that had habituated itself to constant availability, always on, always working. It was good, and Daniel felt the class lean toward him while he said it. Marius finished with his arms crossed and said, "The Torah doesn't even define work. That's the whole problem. The rule is unenforceable."

Daniel stood up. He had expected to feel the floor tilt, the lamp feeling Marius had promised, but instead he felt strangely calm, because he actually knew something now. "You're right that it doesn't define work," he said. "But that's not a flaw you found. That's a question the text itself asks. The Mishnah, the first major written collection of Jewish oral law, was compiled around 200 CE under Rabbi Judah ha-Nasi, and it's basically the answer, or rather fourteen generations of answers, to the question you just asked. The rule doesn't die because it's vague. It gets interpreted, generation after generation, and the interpretation becomes the practice." He held up his photocopy of the tractate, the thirty-nine categories, and walked the class through melacha as creative labor rather than effort, and watched Marius's arms slowly come uncrossed.

Marius got his rebuttal, and he was honest enough not to pretend he hadn't heard anything. "Fine," he said. "But then it's not one rule. It's whatever the last rabbi says it is. You're defending a moving target." Daniel said that was a real objection and he wasn't going to pretend it wasn't. "But people sign affidavits all the time," he said, "swearing that something happened, and the something depends on words other people defined for them, and we still think the swearing means something. A living rule is like that. It's a promise whose exact shape gets renegotiated." Ms. Chanthavong wrote something on her clipboard and did not say what.

After class Sandrine found him at his locker. "We didn't win," she said. Ms. Chanthavong had called it a draw, which she almost never did, and had asked both sides to write a page on what they still weren't sure of. "What are you going to write?" Sandrine asked. Daniel said he honestly didn't know yet, that the moving target thing bothered him, that maybe a rule that meant everything meant nothing, or maybe that was just what it looked like from outside.

Marius appeared at the end of the hall with his backpack over one shoulder. "For the record," he said, "you didn't convince me it applies to me. But I'm going to ask my grandfather what he does on Saturdays. He never told me it was that complicated." He shifted the strap on his shoulder. "Your uncle's book. Can I see it sometime?" Daniel took out his phone and photographed the photocopy, all four pages of the thirty-nine categories, and sent it across the hallway, and the three of them stood there reading the small print while the buses pulled up outside the windows.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Caramelization is the browning of sugar on its own, without proteins; table sugar begins to caramelize at about 170 degrees Celsius.
story:
The school cooking classroom smelled like bleach and old butter at four in the afternoon, and Charlie had the whole row of stovetops to herself until Jamie came through the door carrying a canvas bag of supplies like a person who intended to stay. Jamie wanted the caramel sauce for the spring showcase, wanted it badly, had already told three people that she was entering a dessert and that Charlie was her partner in this plan whether Charlie had agreed or not. Charlie had not agreed. Charlie was making the sauce for her parents' anniversary dinner on Saturday, and she said so, twice, while weighing white sugar into the heavy pot.

"You can do both," Jamie said, spooning the sugar flat. "One recipe, two causes. That's efficiency."

Aleksandar arrived late, as always, holding the department's only candy thermometer like it was a fragile bird. He clipped it to the pot's rim and peered at it. "The marks only go up in steps of twenty. A hundred sixty, a hundred eighty. Nothing at one seventy."

"Then we interpolate," Charlie said, pointing at the space between the marks. "One seventy is right there, halfway. We watch the sugar instead of the glass."

Mr. Wijaya, who kept the classroom open on Thursdays for students with kitchen-less apartments and, Charlie suspected, for students with kitchen-full homes they preferred to avoid, was at his desk grading with a red pen and a cup of tea. He did not offer advice. He had told them once, in September, that the room was theirs until five o'clock and that mistakes were cheaper than therapy, and then he had gone back to his papers.

The sugar melted slowly, then all at once, going from wet sand to a clear syrup that began, without warning, to darken at the edges. Aleksandar leaned in. "Is that burning?"

"That's caramelization," Charlie said. "The sugar browning on its own, no protein in it, nothing else in the pot. It starts at about one seventy Celsius." She had read it the night before in a library book with a cracked spine, sitting at the kitchen table while her mother texted her father about Saturday and her father texted back a thumbs-up, which in their household was practically a love letter.

"Take it off now," Jamie said. "Now, it's getting dark."

"Not yet. Pale caramel is sweet and boring. Dark caramel has the bitter edge."

"You're guessing," Jamie said. "You're treating your own instinct like data. That's solipsism with a spatula."

"It's judgment," Charlie said, but she lowered the heat, and the bubbling slowed from an angry churn to something calmer, the color of an old penny, then a shade past it. She had thought about the dinner all week, how her parents had been polite to each other since spring in a way that made politeness feel like furniture covered in plastic, and how a sauce made carefully, in a classroom, by their daughter, might mean more than a store cake. Aleksandar had pointed out that a sauce could not fix anything. Charlie had pointed out that she knew that. Both of them were right, which was the problem.

She poured in the cream at the last second, off the heat, and the pot hissed and swelled and became a sauce, glossy and smelling of toasted sugar and hot butter. Jamie tasted it from the wooden spoon and closed her eyes. "Okay. You're in the showcase. I already put your name on the form."

"You what."

"I needed a partner by Thursday or they drop me. I'll carry it if you're busy Saturday." Jamie said it fast, staring at the pot instead of Charlie, and Charlie understood that the showcase mattered to Jamie in some way she hadn't explained and wasn't going to, something about proving something to an aunt, or to herself, and that being dropped would have cost more than Jamie would say out loud.

Then Aleksandar's phone buzzed, and he held it up, wincing. "So, twist. My mom just texted your mom. She's making a cake for the anniversary. She assumed you'd forgotten."

Charlie stood very still, the spoon dripping back into the pot, the sauce landing in slow amber ribbons. The vestigial timer on the wall, which hadn't worked in years but still hung there with its dead face, looked back at her like a monument to plans nobody consulted. Her mother thought she'd forgotten. Or her mother had wanted, for reasons of her own, to be the one who made something.

"Fine," Charlie said finally. "Then we bring both. Cake and sauce. Nobody has to choose." She found a jar in the supply cabinet, washed it twice, and poured the caramel in while it was still warm enough to flow, and Jamie washed a second jar without being asked, and filled it for the showcase, and labeled them SAUCE 1 and SAUCE 2 in her slanted handwriting.

Mr. Wijaya looked up once, saw the two jars glowing on the counter in the late light, and raised his teacup an inch.

"Halfway between the marks," Aleksandar said, tapping the thermometer. "You called it."

"Call it again Saturday," Charlie said, screwing the lid down tight.

activity: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
knowledge_domain: to build a portfolio of ten artworks around a single theme with an artist's statement
fact: An artist's statement is written in the first person by the artist to explain the ideas, methods and context behind a body of work.
story:
The clay extruder at the back of the community studio had a hand crank, and by the third Saturday of winter Natalie had learned that if she fed a wedge of terracotta through the rectangular die, she could extrude ribbons that came out looking like something between a ribbon and a scar. She had been avoiding it for weeks because Kayden, who shared the studio's Tuesday slot, called it "the pasta machine," and something about that seemed to cheapen what she was trying to do.

What she was trying to do was the portfolio. Ten artworks around one theme, plus a written statement, due to the provincial review board in March. Mr. Ross, who ran the studio on weekends and taught nothing else, had laid out the requirements in October with the flatness of a man reciting a form. "Ten pieces, one theme, one page of writing in your own voice." Natalie had nodded and then gone home and produced nine pages of notes about her theme, which was doors, and no actual doors.

The trouble was the writing. She had drafted her statement six times, and each draft sounded like a museum label for someone else's work. "The artist is interested in thresholds," the first draft began. "The artist uses clay because it remembers pressure." She read it aloud in the studio kitchen while Maina rinsed brushes and did not react, which was itself a reaction. Maina had a way of letting silence do the work, and it worked.

"Do you talk like that?" Maina finally said.

"I'm being professional."

"You sound like a placard." Maina shook out a brush and set it bristles-up in the jar. "My aunt does those for a living. Writes the little cards. For other people's art, though."

That night, waiting for the bus, Natalie remembered something she hadn't thought about in years, a memory that surfaced the way the terracotta ribbons did, pressed through a shape she hadn't chosen. In grade four, her grandmother had taught her to make bread, and when Natalie asked how she'd know it was done, her grandmother had said, "I just know," and Natalie had thought that was cheating, that there must be a rule somewhere, a timer, a temperature, something a stranger could read off a card. She had spent a whole afternoon trying to write down the rule. Her grandmother had watched her do it and laughed until she had to sit down, not cruelly, just delighted, and said, "You want to hand me a piece of paper to tell me what my hands already know."

On Sunday she brought the drafts to Mr. Ross, who was loading the kiln and did not look up. "Where's your voice in this?" he asked, which was the kind of question she hated because it could mean anything.

"The theme is doors. It's not about me."

He straightened, wiped his hands, and tapped the page. "An artist's statement is written in the first person by the artist to explain the ideas, methods and context behind a body of work. First person. That's the whole point. It's you explaining you."

Natalie stood there holding her nine pages and felt something rearrange, not a revelation exactly, more like a door that had been unlocked the entire time and she'd been leaning on it. All those drafts where she'd written "the artist" as if the artist were a stranger she admired from a distance, as if calling herself an artist too directly would be a kind of theft. She had a nascent suspicion that the distance was the problem, that the committee didn't want a placard, they wanted the person whose hands had cranked the extruder until her palm ached.

She sat at the work table and wrote without drafting, which frightened her. "I make doors because I grew up in a house where every door had a trick to it," she wrote, and stopped, because that was true and she hadn't known she was going to say it. The jammed bathroom door, the cellar door you had to lift on its hinges, her father's study, closed. She kept going. She wrote about the extruder, how you feed the clay through and it comes out changed but continuous, still the same clay, and how that seemed to her like a postulate she was testing rather than a fact she could prove, that a person passes through doors and stays themselves.

When she read it to Maina the following Tuesday, Maina listened all the way through and then said, "That's the first one where I'd know you in a hallway."

Kayden, cranking the extruder with a fresh wedge of clay, looked over. "Okay, but is it art or is it therapy?"

"I don't know yet," Natalie said, and meant it, and found she could say that now without it feeling like failure. "Maybe the not knowing is part of the statement."

She fed a ribbon of terracotta through the die and pressed it against the half-built door she'd been avoiding for a month, a door with no house around it, standing alone on a slab. Maina held the ribbon steady while Natalie scored the join, and the two of them worked without talking until the studio lights flickered, which meant Mr. Ross was closing up.

On the way out, Kayden called from the doorway, "Frame the not knowing, then."

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: North Dakota is the only US state without voter registration; it abolished registration in 1951, and voters instead show identification at the polls.
story:
The line outside the elementary school gymnasius moved slowly, and Jack kept folding and unfolding the piece of paper in his jacket pocket as though it might change what it said. It was a letter from the county election office, informing him that his application to vote had never been received, and that in this state one could not simply walk in and be counted. He had read it four times on the bus. Four years ago, when he was sixteen, he had stood in almost exactly this kind of line beside his father outside the fire hall in their old town, too young to do anything but watch, and his father had never needed a piece of paper to prove he belonged there. Nobody did.

Ahead of him, Alessio was arguing softly with a poll worker, holding up his phone. "I moved here in August," Alessio was saying. "From North Dakota. Nobody ever registered me for anything in my life." The poll worker, a stoic woman with reading glasses on a chain, shook her head with the patience of someone who had answered this question a hundred times and would answer it a hundred more. Jack felt something shift in his chest, a recognition that arrived before the thought did.

"You're from North Dakota?" Jack asked, when Alessio stepped out of the line to call his mother. Alessio turned. He had that look Jack knew from the first week of school, the look of a person perpetually one form away from being a person here. "Fargo," Alessio said. "Three months ago."

"Same," Jack said. "Well, not Fargo. Bismarck, six years, and before that here. That's why I thought I was fine." He pulled out the letter and showed him. "My dad never registered either. Not once. North Dakota doesn't have it at all. They abolished registration in 1951, and it's the only state in the country without it. You just show ID at the polls." Saying it out loud, he heard how it must sound to someone from anywhere else, like describing a place where gravity worked sideways.

Alessio squinted at the letter. "So what do we do?"

"There's same-day registration inside. I checked. You need proof of address." Jack patted his pocket, where his utility bill and his lease sat folded next to the letter, preparations he had made at the last minute because some part of him still believed he wouldn't need them. When he was sixteen, his father had been intransigent about exactly this kind of thing, refusing on principle to carry documents he considered an insult, and there had been an argument at the fire hall, quiet but hard, the kind where nobody yells and everybody loses. His father had won that day, in the sense that he had voted without bowing to anything. Jack had eulogized that stubbornness for years, admired it, repeated it at dinner tables, and only in the last month, holding the county's rejection letter, had he begun to wonder whether his father's pride had been a principle or just the luxury of never having been told no.

Mr. Sun was working the check-in table, of all people, his old tenth grade history teacher, now with a badge on a lanyard instead of chalk on his sleeves. "Jack," Mr. Sun said, and then, reading the screen more carefully, "Jack. There's a hold on your record." The gymnasium smelled of floor wax and coffee. Behind Jack, the line pressed closer.

"I know," Jack said. "I never registered. I thought I didn't have to." He laid the lease on the table, the utility bill, his license with the old Bismarck address still on it. "We came from a place where you didn't. Alessio too. It's not an excuse, it's just where we're from."

Mr. Sun took the papers and began the slow clerical ritual, typing, stamping, initialing, and Jack stood there with his hands empty, watching a stranger's careful pen decide whether he existed here. It was not the clean defiance his father would have wanted for him. It was paperwork, and humility, and a willingness to be entered into a book he had never needed before. Whether that made him more practical than his father or merely less brave, he genuinely did not know, and he suspected the answer would take longer than one election to find.

Alessio appeared at his elbow, breathless, waving a bank statement printed at the library. "They let me," he said. "I'm in. I can actually vote." He was grinning the way he hadn't grinned all semester, and Jack, still waiting on Mr. Sun's stamp, felt the grin arrive on his own face before he had decided anything about it. "Go," Jack said. "Save me a spot at the machines."

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: White coat hypertension is when blood pressure reads high in a clinic, often from nervousness, but normal at home, so doctors may check it with home or all-day monitoring.
story:
Marcus had never once in his life been nervous at the dentist, which was why the number on the little screen annoyed him so much. 152 over 94. He was seventeen, sat in a molded chair under fluorescent light with a paper bib clipped around his neck, and the hygienist had wrapped the cuff around his arm as routinely as she might have checked his chart. She frowned at the screen, tapped it, and said they'd take it again at the end. Marcus told her he was fine. He was, in fact, completely fine, and he said this in a voice slightly louder than the room required.

The appointment was a cleaning, but it was also, inconveniently, research. His biology teacher had assigned a presentation for Friday, three days away, on how diet and exercise change blood pressure, and Marcus had planned to interview his own dentist and walk out with a tidy data point: here is a normal teenager, here is his normal reading, observe how sodium and sedentary living do or do not appear. The plan had seemed almost axiomatic when he'd made it. Seventeen-year-olds did not have high blood pressure. He had a biology textbook that said so in a paragraph he'd underlined twice.

The second reading, near the end of the appointment, was 148 over 91. The dentist, a small dry woman with reading glasses pushed up into her hair, said they'd note it and that he should mention it to his family doctor, and then, because Marcus was staring at the screen with his mouth full of suction, she added that it happened fairly often in her chair. "Teeth, drills, needles," she said. "People climb the walls quietly. The cuff sees it anyway."

He walked out with a printed slip of paper, which felt like evidence against himself. On the bus he texted Karan, whose father had had a heart attack two winters ago and whose house consequently contained a home blood pressure monitor, an ominous beige box that had once presaged, for Karan's whole family, every anxious evening for a year. Karan texted back a single sentence: come over, we'll do it properly.

Properly meant Marcus sitting at Karan's kitchen table while Karan's mother made tea and tried not to hover, which she did anyway, tea being her version of hovering. The home readings, taken twice, ten minutes apart, were 122 over 76 and then 118 over 74. Marcus looked at the numbers on the little screen and felt something rearrange itself in his head. High in the chair, normal at the table. Same arm, same boy, one day apart. He had walked into Karan's house half-believing he was sick and walked to the counter to get a better look believing something more complicated, though he couldn't yet say what.

He spent that evening on his laptop, skimming medical sites and discarding the ones with ads for supplements, and found the phrase he needed. White coat hypertension. He said it aloud to himself, twice, the way you test whether a word will hold weight in your mouth. Blood pressure that reads high in the clinic, often from nervousness, but normal at home, and so doctors might check it with home readings or all-day monitoring rather than trusting one number from one chair. He copied nothing down verbatim, because the assignment was supposed to be his own, but he understood it well enough to rebuild it from scratch, which is what he did in his notebook, in pencil, drawing two columns: clinic and home.

The presentation was Friday morning and Marcus finished the slides Thursday at midnight, which was its own small form of ascetic discipline, no phone, no music, just the laptop and a glass of water. He had decided, against the advice of both Karan and Dimitrios, to open with his own numbers. Dimitrios, who had reviewed the slides over lunch and who believed in clean narratives the way some people believe in luck, said it would muddy things, that the teacher would think Marcus was making the project about himself. "That's what it's about," Marcus said, and then, less certainly, "partly."

Standing at the front of the room, he put up the two readings side by side, 152 over 94 and 122 over 76, and told the class the truth in the order he'd learned it: first the chair, then the table, then the name for the difference. He explained how aerobic exercise over months lowers resting pressure, how sustained high sodium intake raises it, how the vessels and the heart adapt in slow conversation with each other, and then he stopped and said the part he'd argued with himself about including. "One thing I can't tell you," he said, "is which of my numbers is the real one. Or whether that's even the right question. Maybe a reading is always about where you are when it's taken." Mr. Sow, who taught down the hall and had drifted in to listen from the back, raised his eyebrows at that, and Marcus couldn't read the expression, and the bell rang before he could decide whether to ask.

After class, Karan caught him at the door. "So are you going to the doctor or not?" Marcus folded the printout of his clinic reading, the slip with the frowning number on it, and put it in his back pocket instead of the trash, where he'd been planning, all week, to put it. "Monday," he said. "I'll ask about the all-day monitor thing." Then he zipped his bag and went to find out if the cafeteria had anything without fries.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: When parking facing downhill next to a curb, turning the front wheels toward the curb means the car will roll into the curb, not into traffic, if the brakes fail.
story:
The parking lot behind the Food Fair was empty on Sunday mornings, which was exactly why Aaron's father had chosen it, and why Mr. Visser agreed to meet them there with his old sedan and a thermos of coffee that steamed through the cracked lid. Aaron had failed his first driving test in June for two things: the parallel park, which he had abandoned halfway and apologized for, and the highway merge, where he had slowed to forty kilometres an hour at the bottom of the ramp while a transport truck bore down on the Corolla's rear bumper like a verdict. Mr. Visser, who had retired from teaching shop class and now spent his mornings being irascible about municipal bike lanes, had offered to supervise the second attempt at learning.

"Guneet passed on her first try," Sharon said from the curb, where she and Guneet had come to watch, supposedly to buy chips and actually to heckle. "She parallel parked between two shopping carts."

"Shopping carts don't have feelings," Guneet said. "Cars judge you."

Mr. Visser set out four milk crates where the test cones would go and stood beside them, gesticulating at the space between with both hands as though he were conducting an orchestra that refused to listen. "You're not parking a car, you're parking a space. The car is just the thing that fills it." Aaron had heard a version of this from his father, who framed it as patience, and from a YouTube instructor who framed it as geometry, angles of approach measured against the rear tire, and he had never quite managed to hold both ideas at once. Patience told him to go slow. Geometry told him to commit to the angle early and not correct it into a wobble.

He tried it the patient way first, creeping in at walking speed, adjusting, adjusting again, and ended up a metre from the curb with the wheel turned the wrong direction entirely. Mr. Visser made a noise like a kettle. On the next attempt Aaron committed, swung in sharper than felt safe, and felt the back tire kiss the curb, not hard, just a tap, and when he straightened out he was close, genuinely close, maybe thirty centimetres, which was passing distance.

"Better," Mr. Visser said. "Now, one thing before you get out." He pointed at the front wheels. "This lot slopes. Look at it, it runs down toward the street. If you're parking facing downhill next to a curb, which way do you turn the front wheels?"

Aaron looked at the wheels, then at the curb, then at the street below, where a delivery van was idling. His first instinct was away from the curb, toward the road, which felt like freedom, like steering toward escape if something went wrong. But escape for the car meant rolling into traffic. He thought of the van. He turned his hands on the invisible wheel the other way.

"Toward the curb," he said. "Facing downhill, you turn them toward the curb. Then if the brakes ever fail, the car rolls into the curb, not into traffic." Saying it aloud, he could see it whole: the slope, the wheels, the small deliberate choice to point the car at the thing that would stop it.

"Correct," Mr. Visser said, and drank his coffee as though he had never doubted it, which they all knew was a performance.

They drove to the on-ramp after, Sharon in the back pretending to read Guneet's palm, and Aaron came down the ramp at speed this time, signalling early, matching the flow, sliding into a gap between a hatchback and a florist's van with his heart going but his hands steady. Nobody applauded, which was somehow the right response. On the way back he parallel parked on an actual street, on an actual hill, between an actual parked car and a fire hydrant, and turned the wheels toward the curb before he even thought about whether he should. Guneet leaned out the window toward a woman waiting at the crosswalk and said, "He's an aesthete of the three-point turn," and the woman laughed, and Aaron, pulling out cleanly, decided he would take it as a compliment.

"Test is Thursday," his father said that night, keys on the table between them. Aaron nodded, and did not say he was ready, and did not say he wasn't. He picked up the keys and turned them over once, looking at the groove down the middle, and put them in his pocket.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Form V cocoa butter crystals melt at about 33.8 degrees Celsius, just below body temperature, which is why well-tempered chocolate melts in the mouth but not in the hand.
story:
Ms. Bouchard set the marble slab on the counter and told them that today they would learn patience, or at least chocolate, and that in this room the two were the same thing. Justine tied her apron tighter and watched her teacher pour a ribbon of melted dark chocolate onto the cold stone. It spread like something alive, glossy and loose, and then, as Ms. Bouchard drew the spatula through it again and again, it began to thicken, to lose its shine, to look almost matte at the edges. "You're cooling it on purpose," Muhammad said from the next station, and Ms. Bouchard said only, "Watch," and kept working.

Justine got her own slab. The recipe card said to melt the chocolate to forty-five degrees, then cool it on the marble while stirring, then warm it gently back to working temperature, and it warned that if she overheated it she would have to begin again. She had read the card twice the night before and understood almost none of it. What she wanted, and could not have said why she wanted it so badly, was the thing Ms. Bouchard had shown them at the start of class: a bar snapped clean in half, a bright crack through the room, a shine you could see your face in. Justine's mother sent a remittance every month from three provinces away, and in the last envelope there had been a photograph of herself outside a factory in the cold, and Justine had thought, without planning to, that she would mail her mother something made by her own hands, something beautiful and precise, before Christmas.

The stirring was interminable. Muhammad worked beside her, humming, while Kyleigh at the far station kept lifting her spatula to check whether her chocolate had changed yet, which it had not, because she kept lifting it. "You have to leave it alone," Justine said, and Kyleigh said, "It's boring," and Justine said, "That's kind of the point," and kept her own eyes down, drawing the chocolate from the centre out, folding it back, feeling the stone drink the heat out of it through the spatula.

At the farmers' market on Saturday, which was where this whole thing had started, Justine had stood with Kyleigh and Muhammad at a chocolatier's table and asked the man there why his bars sat solid in the sun on a warm June table and still melted the second they touched her tongue. He had tapped his temple and said, "Form V," and told them that Form V cocoa butter crystals melt at about 33.8 degrees Celsius, just below body temperature, which was why well-tempered chocolate melted in the mouth but not in the hand. Kyleigh had bought two bars with her last five dollars. Muhammad had expostulated all the way home about how chocolate was basically engineering, and Justine had said nothing, but she had gone home and looked up their school's Foods elective and found that Ms. Bouchard taught the chocolate unit in November.

Now, at her station, she brought the cooled chocolate back over the double boiler for seconds at a time, testing a dab on her lip the way the card said, hunting for the narrow window where it was fluid but not hot, where the crystals Ms. Bouchard kept calling "the good ones" would survive. She thought about her mother's photograph, about how her mother had never once in her life tempered anything, and she thought about Muhammad's engineering, and both ways of seeing it felt true at once: it was chemistry you could not argue with, and it was also care, the slow kind, the kind you could not rush without ruining. She could not have said which one mattered more, and she decided she did not have to decide.

She dipped the corner of a knife and set the drop on parchment to test it. Kyleigh leaned over her shoulder, chin almost in Justine's hair, and Justine did not push her away, only angled the parchment so they could both see. "If it's right, it sets in about three minutes and it's shiny," Justine said. "If it's wrong, it goes dull and bends." They waited. Muhammad drifted over with his own test drop and set it beside hers without a word, and the three of them stood at the counter like people waiting for a bus that might not come.

The drop set. Justine peeled it off the parchment and held it up to the window light and it shone, an even glassy shine, and she snapped it in two and the crack was clean and small and real. Kyleigh laughed out loud. Muhammad clapped once, then looked embarrassed and put his hands in his apron pocket. Justine laid the two halves on her palm and they lay there, solid, unbothered, exactly as they had on the market table in June, and then she put one half on her tongue and closed her mouth, and waited.

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
knowledge_domain: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
fact: In England, a tenancy deposit is capped at five weeks' rent when the annual rent is under 50,000 pounds, and at six weeks' rent when it is 50,000 pounds or more.
story:
Luke spread the two leases across the kitchen table while his mother boiled the kettle for the third time that evening, neither of them saying anything about the divorce paperwork stacked on the counter. The first flat, above the chip shop on Harehills Lane, charged £650 a month plus a £120 utilities estimate, and the landlord wanted a deposit of £1,000. The second, a room in a shared house near Ms. Hughes's place, was £550 a month with water included and a deposit of £690. Luke had told his mother he would work out the true monthly cost of each, and he meant to do it properly, the way Ms. Hughes had shown him when she came round with a casserole and stayed to look at the paperwork.

"Add everything that recurs," she had said, tapping the gas estimate, the internet, the council tax band. "Then look once at what you pay up front, because that's where they catch you." She hadn't said anything else, just left him with the numbers and a slice of lemon cake wrapped in foil.

He made two columns. Flat one came to £650 plus £120 utilities plus £35 internet plus £95 council tax, which was £900 a month before he'd bought a single tin of beans. Flat two came to £550 plus £70 for gas and electric plus £35 internet plus £78 council tax, £733 all in. He sat back. The chip shop flat was nicer, he thought, all those tall windows, and then he thought about £167 a month, which was two thousand a year, which was most of what he'd saved from the garden centre.

Then he looked at the deposits again. £1,000 on a £650 flat felt large, but he had no instinct for what was normal. He texted Braedon, who had moved out in September and had learned everything the hard way.

The reply came while Luke was washing up. "look up the deposit cap rules," Braedon wrote. "it's capped at five weeks rent if the yearly rent is under 50 grand. six weeks if it's 50 grand or more." Luke dried his hands and did the arithmetic. £650 a month was £7,800 a year, comfortably under £50,000, so the most the landlord could take was five weeks of rent. Five weeks was 650 divided by 4.33, roughly £150 a week, times five, £751. The £1,000 being asked was well over. He checked the second flat the same way: £550 monthly was £6,600 a year, also under the threshold, and five weeks came to about £635, so the £690 there was also too high, though only by £55. Both landlords, or both letting agents, had rounded upward in their own favour.

His mother came in and read his figures over his shoulder. "So the cheap one's actually cheaper," she said. "Even after the deposit?" Luke said yes, and then said the strange part out loud: the deposit wasn't really a cost, since it came back, but it was money he had to have, and the cap told him what he had to have it for. She remonstrated gently with the letting agent on the phone the next morning, and a woman on the other end said she'd "look into it," in the tone of someone who already knew.

Allie came round that afternoon with her own lease in her bag, because she was trying to decide between two studios and had heard, through Luke's message to the group chat, that he'd become the person who knew about this. They sat at the same table and she watched him carry the weekly rent out to the deposit figure, then argue with herself about whether the more expensive flat was worth it for the light, for the quiet street, for the walk along the canal. "You can't put a number on the canal," she said. "You can put a number on everything else, though," Luke said, and she laughed and stole a corner of the lemon cake.

He thought about his philosophy teacher saying that phenomenology meant describing the thing as it appears to you, not as the theory says it must be, and it occurred to him that this was what he was doing with the flats: laying out how each one actually appeared in pounds per month, rather than how it appeared in the photographs, all boreal light and throws draped over beds that would not be his. The chip shop flat still pulled at him. He could admit that. The numbers said one thing and the tall windows said another, and he did not know yet which voice he trusted, only that he now knew exactly what each flat would cost him down to the last standing charge.

On Thursday a letter came from the second letting agent, a proper letter on paper, confirming that the deposit would be reduced to £634.92, "in line with the applicable cap." Luke read it twice at the kitchen table, then propped it against the fruit bowl where his mother would see it. He still hadn't signed anything. He picked up his pen, drew a box around the £733, and drew a smaller, wavering box around the £900.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: The US fairness doctrine, introduced in 1949, required broadcasters to air contrasting views on controversial public issues; the Federal Communications Commission abolished it in 1987.
story:
Maelie had the transcript open on one half of the screen and her notes on the other, and the two halves were refusing to agree. For her history seminar she had to compare how three outlets covered the mill shutdown on the river, the one her uncle had worked at for eleven years. One story called the closure "a strategic realignment." Another called it "a gutting of the town." A third barely mentioned the town at all. Paula had texted her twice from her own kitchen, a few streets over: did you find the fourth source yet, and, later, my dad says they're all owned by the same two companies, is that true.

Maelie clicked through the ownership pages. The first outlet belonged to a holding company that also ran the paper mill's biggest customer. The second was owned by a family whose name appeared on the renovation plaque at the library, donors to everything, friends of everyone. She sat back. Outside the window the maple had gone fully arboreal again after the winter, its canopy shutting out the streetlight in patches, and she watched a neighbor's cat pick its way along the fence beneath it.

She called her grandmother, because her grandmother had opinions about the news the way other people had opinions about weather. "I'm doing this assignment," Maelie said, phone on speaker, hands still on the keyboard. "And I keep finding that whoever owns the outlet seems to matter."

"Of course it matters," her grandmother said. "It always mattered. Though when I was young, the TV stations had to air both sides. There was a fairness doctrine, they called it. Came in 1949. The FCC abolished it in 1987, and after that everything got louder."

Maelie typed it into the search bar while her grandmother went on about Walter Cronkite. The fairness doctrine, she read, required broadcasters to air contrasting views on controversial public issues. She had assumed the loud, lopsided news landscape was just how things had always been, and the screen quietly disabused her of that. There had been a rule, and then there wasn't.

"That's the thing, though," she said, mostly to herself, and her grandmother waited, which she was good at. "If someone owns the station, couldn't they just make both sides sound bad? Or pick the weakest person to argue the side they don't like?" The doctrine said contrasting views had to air. It didn't say who chose them, or how honestly. She wrote that in her notes and then crossed out the word "honestly" and wrote "carefully," because honestly was a judgment and she hadn't earned it yet.

Paula arrived at four with her backpack and half a bag of chips, and they spread the printouts across the bed. "My dad says follow the money," Paula said, dropping into the desk chair. "But my dad also thinks the moon landing was staged, so."

"So he's a confounder," Maelie said, and Paula laughed. "No, listen. He's right for a reason he can't explain, which is worse than being wrong. Ownership is part of it. But the third outlet is independently owned and it still barely covered us. Maybe small papers just don't have reporters anymore." She laid the three articles side by side. "So here's my thesis. Ownership shapes what gets covered, and it shaped at least one of these for sure. But it isn't the only force, and I can't prove which force did what in the other two. I'll say that."

"That's not a thesis, that's a shrug," Paula said, but she was reading the ownership page, chin in her hand, and she stopped chewing. "Wait. The mill's biggest customer owns the first one. That's the one that called it a realignment." She looked up. "Say the shrug part out loud again. I want to put it in my intro."

Maelie read it aloud, and then deleted a sentence from her draft and wrote a better one, the kind that admitted where the evidence ran out. Paula took the printouts to the scanner. Through the window the maple had gone dark except where the streetlight found a gap, and Maelie left the search history on the screen, fairness doctrine, 1949, abolished 1987, in case her mother came by later and wondered what she'd been doing all afternoon.

"Send me the ownership page," Paula said from the hallway, already typing. "I'm going to make my dad read it."

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: According to the CDC, US drivers aged 16 to 19 have a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers aged 20 and older, per mile driven.
story:
The parking lot of the community college was empty except for a soccer coach dragging cones across the far asphalt, and Zachary's mother turned off the engine and dropped the keys into his palm as though handing over something alive. "Six days," she said. "The test is in six days, and then you're driving yourself to orientation whether I like it or not." She got out and walked to the shade of a maple, folding her arms in a way that meant she would rather be anywhere else but could not say so.

He adjusted the mirror, which was already correct, and then adjusted it back. Three weeks ago, at the DMV, he had stood in line behind a girl who kept rereading a poster on the wall while she waited for her permit test. She'd read it out loud to nobody, half under her breath: according to the CDC, drivers aged sixteen to nineteen had a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers aged twenty and older, per mile driven. Three times. He'd done the math on the ride home, sitting in this same seat, and the math hadn't gotten better since.

He started the car. Zayden's text arrived a minute later, a photo of the course schedule with the caption, you better be practicing, because you're driving us both to campus in the fall, no arbitration, this is decided. Zachary laughed, put the phone face down on the passenger seat, and let the clutch out too fast. The car bucked once and died.

"Again," his mother called from the maple, her voice flat as a referee's.

He restarted. This time he found the friction point where the pedal caught, and the car rolled forward, slow and level, and something in his chest unclenched. He drove the length of the lot, turned wide around a light pole, came back. On the third pass he was almost smooth, and he let himself think, briefly, that he might be a natural, that the poster statistic was about other people, the ones who texted and sped and showed off. Then he remembered Elle, who had taken the test in June and failed it for rolling a stop sign, and how she'd said afterward, "I'm honestly the careful one, and I still messed it up." That had stayed with him more than the poster had. If it could happen to Elle, the arithmetic probably didn't care how he saw himself.

He parked crookedly between two faded lines and pulled the brake. His mother got in the passenger side, reaching across to check his seatbelt with one knuckle. "Take us out on Marsh Road," she said. "Low speed. Real road, before the test does it to you first."

Marsh Road was two lanes with a soft shoulder and a ditch that his mother narrated the whole way, as if naming the hazards could exonerate her from the decision to let him near them. A delivery van appeared in the mirror, riding close, and Zachary's hands went rigid on the wheel. He checked the speedometer: twenty-eight in a thirty-five. The van honked once, gratuitous, since there was a clear passing lane the whole time, and swung around them. His mother said nothing, which was somehow louder.

"Zayden wants me to drive us to campus in the fall," he said, eyes on the road. "And you want me driving myself to orientation. And I keep thinking about that poster at the DMV. Almost three times, per mile. That's not nothing." His mother turned to look at him, and he kept going before she could answer. "But everyone I know learned on this road, and they're all fine, and I have to learn sometime. So I don't know which one I actually believe. Maybe both."

She was quiet for a quarter mile. "Left signal before the stop sign," she said finally. "Check the mirror first." He signaled, checked, stopped fully with the nose of the car just behind the white line, and waited while an old sedan crossed in front of them, its driver an oblivious and unhurried stranger. Then he turned left, smooth, onto the wider street, and felt the wheel go light and willing under his hands, and behind them the sun came off the windshield of the car following, close and patient in the mirror.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first instant replay on television was shown by CBS during the Army-Navy football game on December 7, 1963, using a system devised by director Tony Verna.
story:
The living room smelled of burnt popcorn and chili, and by the third quarter every seat was taken, so Victoria sat on the arm of the couch with her plate balanced on her knee. Her father had invited the neighbors over for the championship, which meant Mr. Krause from two doors down was already shouting at the screen, and Kyla had arrived with Omar and a bag of tortilla chips she refused to share until halftime. On the television, the running back dove for the pylon and the ball popped loose just as his knee hit, and the whole room rose at once, some of them yelling touchdown and the rest yelling fumble.

"That was down by contact," Omar insisted, standing so fast he knocked a soda can. "They have to review it."

"They'll show it again," Kyla said. "They always show it again."

But the referee's voice came through the speakers announcing the ruling on the field, and before anyone could settle back down, Mr. Krause made a low sound of disgust. "You know what ruined this game? Instant replay. All of it. Growing up, the call was the call, and you argued about it over Sunday dinner and that was that. Now everybody in the country thinks they're the official." He pointed his beer at the screen. "Half these arguments are about the camera, not the game."

Victoria's little cousin, who had been permitted to stay up on the condition of perfect behavior, was near tears because he was certain the runner had scored, and her mother was trying to soothe him while also passing out the chili she'd been warming since noon. Her mother had come home late from the clinic, where she'd spent the afternoon giving flu shots, and she was still explaining to anyone who'd listen that the shot worked by teaching the immune system to recognize a piece of the virus, a harmless fragment called an antigen, so the body would be ready for the real thing. Victoria had heard the explanation so many times she could have delivered it herself, though she noticed nobody at the party was actually listening, least of all Mr. Krause.

The argument about the play was not really about the play anymore. Omar had his phone out, replaying the broadcast's slow-motion angle, frame by frame, and Mr. Krause kept saying it didn't matter what the phone showed, and Kyla was arguing that if the technology existed you'd be a fool not to use it, and Victoria's father was trying to referee the referees with his palms raised. Her cousin sniffled into his sleeve. Victoria set down her plate.

"Mr. Krause," she said, "when did they start doing replays? On TV, I mean. You said you grew up without them."

"Some time in the sixties," he said, waving it off. "I was a kid. Before your father was born, I'll tell you that much."

Victoria pulled out her phone, but the argument rolled on behind her, so she went into the hallway where it was quieter and typed carefully, wanting the actual answer rather than the first loud one. What she found made her sit down on the bottom stair. Then she came back and stood in the middle of the room, and because everyone was mid-shout, she held up the phone like a referee signaling a timeout, which, to her surprise, worked.

"Okay, so nobody's right exactly, but Mr. Krause's close." She read it out. "The first instant replay on television was shown by CBS during the Army-Navy football game on December 7, 1963. It was a system devised by the director, Tony Verna." She looked at Mr. Krause. "So it's not quite your whole childhood. You'd have been watching games before that with no replay at all, and then one day, this."

"Army-Navy," Mr. Krause repeated, and something in his face shifted, like he was locating a room in a house he hadn't visited in years. "December of sixty-three. I remember that game. My father had the radio on, and then the next week the whole neighborhood was at the TV for it." He scratched his jaw. "Verna. Huh."

"So the arguments are older than you," Kyla said, grinning. "People have been fighting about the camera for sixty years."

"That's not what I said," Mr. Krause said, but without heat, and then he turned to Omar, who still had the slow motion frozen on his screen. "All right, show me the frame. But understand I'm watching it as a skeptic."

They bent over the phone together, the two of them, and Victoria watched Mr. Krause's finger tap the edge of the screen as Omar stepped it forward. "There," Omar said. "Knee down, then the ball comes out."

"That's not nothing," Mr. Krause admitted. "It's not the whole truth either, but it's not nothing." Her cousin had crept over to look too, forgetting his tears entirely, and her mother came back from the kitchen with more chili and stood in the doorway smiling at all of them crowded around a five-inch screen while the actual game, unwatched, played itself out on the big one.

Later, after the neighbors had gone home and Kyla and Omar were pulling on their coats, Victoria stood at the sink rinsing plates and thinking about the day her mother had described, the one where the body learns from a harmless fragment how to face the real thing. There was a version of the evening where everyone just kept yelling, and a version where an old memory and a new frame got held side by side, and she still wasn't sure which she believed in, whether the camera had underpinned the game or bent it. It was probably both, and probably not hers to settle. Her father came in with the last of the glasses and set them beside her.

"Nice save on the replay thing," he said.

"I mostly just read a sentence," she said.

"Mostly," he said, and handed her the dish towel.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: ISO 216 paper sizes such as A4 have sides in the ratio of 1 to the square root of 2, so cutting a sheet in half gives two sheets of the same shape.
story:
Hannah had promised the environmental club a poster by Friday, and by Wednesday afternoon the poster existed only as a drawing on A3 paper, pinned to the drying rack in Ms. Shapiro's room, its gouache still tacky in the corners. The club wanted it smaller, small enough to tape inside bathroom stalls, and larger, large enough to read from the back of the gym. Two versions, then, and she had no idea how to make one design become two sizes without starting over.

"Photocopy it," Ellis said, not looking up from the coil pot he was scoring with a toothpick. "The machine does the thinking."

"That's exactly what I don't like about it," Hannah said, and then heard herself, and laughed. She had been reading about metacognition for a psychology elective, thinking about thinking, and here she was doing it in the ordinary way, noticing that she distrusted a machine for doing hers. "I want to know what happens to a picture when it changes size. Not just that it happens."

She took a fresh sheet of A3 from the cupboard and, because she was avoiding the problem, began trimming it with the guillotine to make placeholder cards. She cut the sheet in half, and then, idly, in half again, and stopped. The halves looked wrong in a way she couldn't name, then right in a way she also couldn't name. She held the original sheet against one of the halves, corner to corner, tilting it against the window light. The shapes matched. Exactly. She tried the smaller pieces, and they matched too, the big and the small nested like Russian dolls, every rectangle the same rectangle at a different scale.

"Jia," she said across the room. "Come look at this and tell me if I'm hallucinating."

Jia came, still wearing one glove of ink. She held the sheets together, turned them over, squinted down the long edge. "They're the same shape. How are they the same shape? I cut things in half all the time and they're never the same shape."

"Because this paper isn't arbitrary," Hannah said slowly, working it out as she spoke. "Someone chose these proportions so this would happen. Cut any sheet like this in half and you get two sheets with the same shape, just smaller. It's some standard, ISO something. My dad's office paper says it on the wrapper."

"ISO 216," said Ms. Shapiro from the kiln corner, without turning around, and Hannah felt a small flare of resentment at being handed the answer, even three words of it. She wanted to arrive there herself.

The feeling passed, or she argued with it until it did. Ms. Shapiro hadn't explained anything; she'd only given the thing a handle. What mattered was what Hannah did with it, and what she did was carry three sheets to the table by the windows and lay her poster drawing over the A3, then hold a half-sheet over her sketchbook, comparing. If the shapes were identical, only scaled, then her design could be scaled the same way. She redrew the poster's border in light pencil on the smaller sheet, checking each proportion against the original, and the drawing fit itself into the new size the way a hand fits into a glove one size down. She had assumed that enlarging and reducing were two separate problems, two kinds of work, and the paper was quietly insisting they could be subsumed into a single act, the way one rule can cover a dozen cases.

"Could you do the gym version the same way?" Jia asked, watching over her shoulder.

"In theory. Two A3s side by side make the bigger size, if I keep the same shape. But I haven't tried it." Hannah said this carefully, because she noticed in herself a wish to overclaim, to say yes, it works, it's solved, when what she actually knew was that it worked once, on one sheet, under window light, on a Wednesday. The rectangle had kept its promise one time. Whether it would keep it again was still an open question, and she found she liked having it open. "Can you hold this down while I check the corners?"

Ellis abandoned his pot and came to press the corner flat while Hannah aligned the half-sheet with the full one, edge to edge, the pencilled border lying over the painted border, matching, matching, and at the last inch drifting a hair off, a millimetre of disagreement she could fix with a steady hand.

"Almost," Jia said.

"Almost," Hannah said, and reached for the pencil.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Malcolm Gladwell's 2008 book Outliers popularized the '10,000-hour rule', though Ericsson later said the quality of practice matters more than any fixed number of hours.
story:
The guitar arrived in February, secondhand, its case smelling faintly of the noxious varnish someone had used to cover a scratch along the body. Joshua had found it at a pawnshop after school, carried it home on the bus pressed between his knees, and set it on his bed where he could look at it while he did homework. He did not touch it that first night. He only looked, the way you might look at a door you had decided to open but not yet opened.

He was sixteen, nearly seventeen, and he had wanted this for a while without ever saying so. His father had played something once, Joshua remembered, a keyboard in the corner of an apartment they no longer lived in, but the memory was soft at the edges and he could not reconstruct whether the sound had been good or only present. On Saturday he tried a chord. The steel bit into his fingertips, the shape collapsed, and the resulting noise did not portend anything like music. He tried again.

At school on Monday, Zayne came by his locker and saw the chord chart open in his notebook. "Guitar?" Zayne said. "You're starting now?" There was nothing cruel in it, only a kind of arithmetic. "Malcolm Gladwell's 2008 book Outliers made that ten-thousand-hour rule famous," Zayne said, leaning against the lockers. "Ten thousand hours to get good at anything. That's years. Starting at seventeen, you'd be, like, thirty before you're decent." He shrugged, generous with the math, and Joshua said nothing because he was doing the math too. It came out the same.

That night he sat on the edge of his bed with the guitar across his lap and his laptop open, hunting through the search results like someone looking for a loophole. He found the book in the library's digital catalogue, and beneath it, references to a researcher named Ericsson, whose work Gladwell had drawn on. Joshua read, then stopped, then read the line again. Ericsson had later said the quality of practice mattered more than any fixed number of hours. Not the hours. The quality. He sat with that for a while, one hand flat on the strings, feeling the small buzz of them against his palm. It did not feel like a loophole. It felt like a different contract. Zayne's version promised that time would carry you; this version demanded that you pay attention while it did.

The next practice, he changed what he was doing. Instead of running through the four chords he half-knew, over and over, he isolated the one place where his fingers always failed, the shift to F, and played only that shift, slowly, watching his hand like a coach watches a player who keeps dropping the ball. He did it forty times. It was the least fun he had ever had with the instrument, and afterward the shift worked, twice, and then a third time, and he laughed out loud alone in his room at how small a thing could feel like that.

Tehya came over Thursday to work on a history project and found him in the living room with the chord chart taped to the wall. She had played violin since she was eight and had opinions. "So it's true then," she said, listening to him stumble through a progression. "The ten-thousand-hour thing." Joshua told her what he'd found, carefully, the way you repeat a rumor you want to be true. "Gladwell popularized it, but Ericsson pushed back on it later. Said quality of practice matters more than any fixed number of hours." Tehya considered this, tuning out a passing siren with one ear, the way musicians do. "That tracks," she said. "I practiced badly for years. My teacher used to call it arbitration between me and the piece, like the metronome was the judge." She tapped the chart. "Slow is the ruling nobody wants."

They practiced together for an hour, and it was better than practicing alone, because she noticed things he did not, the way his wrist locked, the way he held his breath through the hard changes. But afterward, walking her to the door, he did not feel resolved. Maybe Zayne was right about the arithmetic anyway, and the quality argument was just something told to late starters so they would keep going. Maybe both were true at once, and the hours and the attention were two hands on the same instrument, neither sufficient alone. He could not tell yet. He was honest enough with himself to admit that.

He went back to the living room and picked the guitar up again. His fingertips still hurt, and would for a while, and he had decided that this, at least, was information rather than punishment. He set the metronome slow, placed his hand on the neck, and began.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: In Judaism, the closest relatives of the person who died sit shiva, a mourning period of seven days that begins after the burial; the Hebrew word shiva means seven.
story:
The synagogue basement smelled of coffee and cold cuts, and Laura stood near the door holding a plate she did not remember taking. Her grandmother had been buried that morning, and now the folding chairs were arranged in rows, and people kept saying the same word to her, sorry, sorry, as though repetition might sand the edges off it.

Her mother sat on a low box near the front, which someone had explained meant mourning close to the ground. Laura had not wanted to sit there. She had chosen a chair at the back, half behind the coat rack, and watched her mother accept casseroles and silence in equal measure. Across the room her father was excoriating himself in a low voice to an uncle, saying he should have driven down more weekends, that three hours was nothing, that he was a terrible son, and the uncle kept shaking his head and saying nothing back.

Elise appeared in the doorway at four o'clock, holding a paper bag with both hands, like something that might spill. She had never met the grandmother. She had come because Laura had texted her a single word, shiva, and an address, and Elise had looked it up on her phone during chemistry and then walked twenty minutes in the wrong shoes.

"Is this okay?" Elise whispered, lifting the bag. Inside were seven oranges. She had counted them on purpose, she said, because she'd read that the whole thing lasted seven days, that it was called shiva, and that shiva meant seven, and she hadn't known what to bring so she brought one for each day. Laura took the bag and felt her throat close around something that was almost laughter.

"It's okay," she managed. "It's more than okay. Nobody told me the name meant seven until this morning. My mom just kept saying it and I thought it was like, a person's name. Shiva. Like we were waiting for someone to arrive." Elise laughed, then pressed her lips together, then laughed again anyway, and Laura found she could breathe.

They sat on the floor behind the last row of chairs, splitting the first orange, and Laura pointed out the small economies of the room: who refilled the coffee urn without being asked, who kept a hand on her mother's shoulder while talking to someone else entirely, the way her little cousin had appointed himself distributor of napkins and was executing the job with tremendous gravity. Her grandmother would have had opinions about the cold cuts. She had been an epicure of deli specifically, an impassioned one, and would have sent back this sliced turkey on grounds of principle.

"I didn't know if I should even come," Elise said, peeling her orange in one long spiral, which took real patience. "Like whether it's rude to show up if you didn't know her. Whether I should just text you instead." Laura turned this over. She had a disaffected friend from summer camp, Marcus-something, who had sent a message that said literally nothing, just a heart emoji, and she had stared at it for ten minutes feeling something complicated and ungenerous, and she had not replied. "Coming is better," she said finally. "Even if you say the wrong thing. The heart emoji was worse. I don't know why. It was like being handed a receipt for my grief." She wasn't sure that was fair to Marcus. She decided she could be unfair about it for one day.

An elderly woman Laura had never met lowered herself onto the floor beside them with a series of small calculations, took a segment of orange without asking, and said, "Your grandmother played canasta with me for forty years and cheated at least half of them. I want you to know she was very bad at cheating. She'd rearrange her whole face." Laura laughed so suddenly that people in the folding chairs turned around, and her mother, close to the ground in her row, looked over and did not smile, exactly, but something in her shoulders let go by a centimeter.

The light through the high basement windows went from white to gold to the particular gray of a winter afternoon giving up. Elise helped the napkin cousin restock. Laura's father stopped rehearsing his failures long enough to eat half a sandwich. On the way out, Elise pressed the remaining six oranges into Laura's hands, one by one, counting under her breath, and Laura carried them out to the car cradled against her coat like eggs, and put them on the back seat where her grandmother's reading glasses were still sitting in their case.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: To indemnify someone is to promise, in a contract, to compensate them for losses they suffer because of certain acts, often written alongside a promise to 'hold harmless'.
story:
The form arrived folded in thirds, tucked into the envelope with the deposit receipt, and Brooklyn spread it flat on the kitchen table between the salt shaker and her mother's cold coffee. Janessa leaned over her shoulder, chewing the last of a strawberry Pop-Tart, while Danika pulled out the chair across from them and sat with her chin in her hands. The paper said Ridgeview Hall Rental Agreement at the top, and beneath that, in a font two sizes smaller, a wall of clauses.

"There," Brooklyn said, tapping paragraph six. "Read that out loud."

Janessa read it anyway, though she clearly wished she hadn't started. "Renter agrees to indemnify and hold harmless the owners of Ridgeview Hall against any claims, losses or damages arising from..." She trailed off. "Arising from, like, us."

"The fundraiser, not us us." Brooklyn turned the page toward the window light. Outside, a delivery truck idled at the curb, its engine shuddering through the glass. The whole thing had started three weeks ago, when the three of them stood up at the community meeting and offered to run a spring fundraiser for the food bank, and Mr. Bakker, who managed the hall, said he liked their oratory so much he would knock forty dollars off the rental fee. He had been captivated, he said, by the idea of teenagers organizing something for once instead of complaining about it. Now the idea had a form attached, and the form had a paragraph she did not understand.

"What does indemnify mean?" Janessa asked. "Is it like insurance?"

"Look it up," Danika said, and then, in an insouciant tone that Brooklyn suspected covered actual nerves, "or just don't sign it. Who reads these things anyway?"

"I do," Brooklyn said. "Now. Starting now." She pulled her phone out and typed the word in, and the definition assembled itself on the screen a line at a time while Janessa watched over her elbow. To indemnify someone, the dictionary said, was to promise, in a contract, to compensate them for losses they suffered because of certain acts, often written alongside a promise to hold harmless. She read it twice. So the word next to it, harmless, wasn't a separate demand. It was the same promise said two ways, one in the fancy Latinate word and one in plain English.

"So if someone slips on the floor at our fundraiser," she said slowly, "and sues Mr. Bakker, we pay for it."

"With what?" Janessa said. "Our fundraiser money? That's for the food bank."

"Or our parents' money." Brooklyn looked at the signature line at the bottom, a thin ruled blank with her mother's name printed above it. Her mother had said, sure, sign it, it's probably standard, we'll look at it tonight. But she was working the late shift, and the deposit was due tomorrow, and standard was doing a lot of work in that sentence.

Danika reached across the table and turned the form around to face herself. She read paragraph six with her lips moving slightly, then flipped to the last page, then flipped back. "There's no limit anywhere," she said. "It doesn't say up to the deposit or anything. It's just, all losses."

The kitchen smelled like burnt toaster pastry and dish soap. Brooklyn got up, filled the kettle, and set it on the stove, mostly to have something to do with her hands. Through the doorway she could hear her little brother's cartoon in the other room, tinny music and a laugh track.

From the doorway, Danika watched Brooklyn stand at the stove with her back turned, and she thought about how the night before, Brooklyn had stayed late at school to help her carry the poster boards even though it was raining, and how she hadn't mentioned it once since. Danika wasn't good at that kind of thing, at absorbing costs quietly. She said what she thought and let the chips fall. But watching Brooklyn now, holding a pen above a line that could cost her family money, Danika understood that some signatures were heavier than the paper they sat on, and that somebody in the group had to be the one who read the small print, even if reading it made everything harder.
