"We could call him," Danika said. "Mr. Bakker. It's seven. He answers his store phone until eight, my mom says."

"He'll think we're being difficult," Janessa said.

"He'll think we're being careful," Brooklyn said. She put the pen down on the table, and it rolled until it stopped against the salt shaker. She dialed the number off the form's letterhead, and the phone rang four times, long enough for the kettle to start its low hum, before Mr. Bakker's voice came through, saying Ridgeview Rentals, good evening.

"Mr. Bakker, it's Brooklyn, about the fundraiser. Before my mom signs, I have a question about paragraph six."

There was a pause, and then a chair creaked somewhere on the other end of the line. "Nobody's ever called about paragraph six," he said. "Ask me anything."

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Ignoring air resistance, a ball dropped from a table and a ball launched horizontally from the same height hit a level floor at the same time.
story:
The quiz was on Monday, and by Friday afternoon Katherine still could not make the equations obey her. She sat in the back corner of Mr. Tehrani's empty classroom with a worksheet full of cannonballs and baseballs, each one launched at some angle, each one demanding that she find where it would land. She knew the formulas. She had copied them neatly onto an index card, and that was the problem, because copying was not the same as believing.

"You're doing it wrong," Philip said from the doorway, though he had looked at her paper for exactly two seconds.

"Thank you. Tremendous help."

He dropped into the seat across from her and spun the worksheet to face him. "You're treating it like one motion. It's two. Sideways and down. They don't talk to each other."

"That's an idiosyncrasy of yours," Katherine said, "explaining things you don't understand by saying them louder."

"I don't say it louder, I say it again." He did, in fact, say it again, and this time she heard the shape of it, though not yet the truth of it. Sideways and down, two separate accounts kept in two separate ledgers. It sounded specious to her, like a trick for avoiding the real problem. A ball going sideways was still going down, surely, and going down faster perhaps, or slower, because of the sideways part. The whole thing had to be one story.

Aliza arrived with a paper bag from the vending machine and a proposal. "I have two rolls of quarters' worth of practice for you people. Table by the window, two golf balls from the gym closet, and a bet."

The bet was this: Philip claimed that if you dropped one ball off the edge of a table and, at the same instant, launched a second ball horizontally off the same table, the dropped ball would hit the floor first. He said it with total confidence, which was how he said most things. Aliza took the other side, on the grounds that Philip was wrong about nearly everything at least once before breakfast. Katherine refused to commit, which both of them mocked, and which she defended as honesty rather than cowardice, though privately she was not sure the two could always be told apart.

They set it up by the windows at the end of the hall, where the floor was linoleum and the custodian was not yet due. Aliza crouched with her ear nearly touching the tile, because the plan was to listen: two golf balls striking a hard floor make two clicks, and if the clicks are close enough together, the ear can judge. Philip held one ball at the table's edge and set the other on the flat of a ruler, ready to shove it sideways. Katherine stood where she could see both balls at once, and counted them down.

The first time, Philip shoved late, and the clicks came apart, and everyone claimed victory at once. The second time the ruler caught the edge of the table. The third time Aliza laughed at the wrong moment and ruined the count. On the fourth try they got it clean, and what Katherine heard, holding her breath, was not two clicks. It was one. A single knock, both golf balls arriving at the floor together, the dropped one and the launched one, from the same height, at the same instant.

"No," Philip said. "Again."

They ran it nine more times while the light in the hall went from white to gold. Twice the timing failed and the clicks separated, one landing before the other, and each of those times the shove had come late; whenever the release was honest, the sound was one sound. Philip sat down on the floor eventually, his back against the table leg, looking as though something in him needed cauterizing. He had been certain, and certainty, once it bleeds, is hard to stop.

"It's the sideways," Katherine said slowly, and then stopped, because she did not want to say something specious in her turn. She sat down across from him. She thought about the worksheet, the cannonballs, the two ledgers. The dropped ball and the launched ball fall the same way, take the same time, arrive together; the horizontal launch changes where the ball goes, not how long it takes to get down. That was Philip's claim from the doorway, which she had dismissed, and he had arrived at it apparently without ever believing it applied to this. He had held both ideas in his head and never let them meet.

"Can I tell you something embarrassing," Philip said. "I've done this chapter already. Last year, at my old school. I got a B on it."

"You got a B on it," Aliza said, delighted, "and you still bet against it."

"I got a B because I memorized it. I never once thought it was true." He picked up one of the golf balls and turned it over in his fingers. "It can't be true. It feels like the thrown one should get some kind of credit. It's trying harder."

Katherine laughed, and then didn't, because she understood him better than she wanted to admit. She had spent the week trusting her index card over her own ears. There was still something she could not close, though, some gap between hearing one knock and knowing why the knock was one, and she decided she would leave that gap open rather than paper over it with a borrowed sentence. On Monday she would do the problems with the two ledgers, and if the numbers came out strange she would say so instead of smoothing them.

The custodian's cart squeaked at the far end of the hall. Aliza swept both golf balls into her jacket pockets with the speed of a much more experienced criminal, and the three of them walked fast toward the stairwell, and Philip, taking the steps two at a time, said, "Same bet, next week, off the bleachers."

"Off the bleachers," Katherine said, "with a stopwatch and my notebook."

"Scared to trust your ears again?"

"Monday," she said. "I want it written down."

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: The dependency ratio compares people aged under 15 and 65 and over with people aged 15 to 64, estimating how many dependents each working-age person supports.
story:
The trail climbed out of the car park in long switchbacks, and by the second one Alice had stopped looking at the view. In her rucksack, folded twice, was the population pyramid Mr. Georgiou had handed out that morning: a printout for a country she had never heard of until Tuesday, its bars wide at the top, narrow at the base, like a champagne flute standing on a pinhead. Her task, written on the back in his cramped hand, was to decide what that country would need more of in thirty years, schools or nursing homes, and to defend the decision when they reached the ridge.

Eamon walked ahead of her with his own pyramid folded into a paper aeroplane, which he launched off an outcrop every few hundred metres. His country had the opposite shape, a pyramid in the honest old sense, wide at the bottom. "Easy," he said, retrieving the plane from a gorse bush. "Schools. More teachers, more everything. Kids everywhere." He said it the way he said most things, as though the world arranged itself to be answered in one word.

Alice did not answer, because her country refused to be easy. The bars at the top were fat; the bars at the bottom were thin; but the middle, the great trunk of working ages, was thick and would stay thick for a while before it thinned. She tried holding the image in her head as she walked: the shape moving through time like a snake swallowing a meal, the bulge travelling upward. Somewhere on the third switchback she understood that the question was not really about old people or children at all. It was about who carried whom.

"It's called the dependency ratio," she said to Manuel, who had fallen into step beside her and was peeling an orange with his thumbnail. He looked at her. "It compares the people under fifteen and the sixty-fives and over with the people in between, fifteen to sixty-four. How many dependents each working-age person supports." Manuel considered this, spat a pip into the heather, and said that in his house it was three dependents and two workers, and his mother did the arithmetic out loud every time a bill arrived.

That was the moment the abstraction folded itself into something she could carry. Her father had been on furlough two summers ago, and she remembered the kitchen-table conversations, the property tax notice, her mother saying that the schools were asking for more and the pension levy was asking for more and both of them were right. Alice had thought then that it was bad luck. Now, on a hillside with the wind moving the grass in one long silver ripple, she thought it was arithmetic, and that bad luck and arithmetic were not the same thing, though they could feel identical from inside a kitchen.

At the ridge, Mr. Georgiou collected them on a flat shelf of rock below the cairn and asked for positions. Manuel went first and gave a speech about his pyramid that was frankly grandiose, full of "the tide of youth" and "a century of building", and Mr. Georgiou let it run and then said only, "And who pays for the tide?" Manuel blinked. Eamon said schools, teachers, everything, kids. Then it was Alice.

She laid her printout on the rock and weighted it with a stone. She said the country would need nursing homes, eventually, but not yet; that for twenty years the middle bars were strong enough to carry the top, and the money would go further if it went to the care homes now, while the carriers were still numerous. She said the dependency ratio made it possible to see the load before it arrived. Then she stopped, because the honest part was next, and honesty slowed her down. She said she could see the shape but not the speed; a pyramid showed ages, not intentions, and she did not know whether the people in the fat middle would stay, or go, or what a government forty years from now would choose to codify into law when the middle thinned. She said, "The numbers tell you the weight. They don't tell you the will."

Mr. Georgiou said nothing for a moment. Below them the valley lay open, a village with a school and a church and, near the road, a low building with a ramp that she had not noticed on the way up. "Same country, more or less," he said. "Different century." They ate lunch on the shelf of rock, and Eamon flew his plane off the cairn into the updraft, where it circled twice and held, for a few seconds, perfectly still.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: US food safety agencies say chicken is safely cooked when its internal temperature reaches 165 degrees Fahrenheit, about 74 degrees Celsius, measured with a food thermometer.
story:
The oven in her grandmother's kitchen ran hot on the left side, a fact Ashley had learned at eleven and never forgotten, and she turned the pan of chicken breasts halfway through roasting because of it. She had volunteered for this dinner the way you volunteer for something you're afraid of, quickly, before the fear could metabolize into an excuse. Her grandmother was back from the hospital on Thursday. Her parents would arrive at seven. Christina had texted twice asking how it was going, and Ashley had answered with a photo of the parsley she'd chopped too fine, because that was easier than admitting the truth, which was that she did not entirely know how to tell when chicken was done.

Her grandmother watched from the stool by the window, her hands folded, offering comments like weather reports. The cast iron was in the lower cabinet. The good olive oil was not for cooking, it was for finishing. Ashley accepted both corrections and kept moving, and when she cut into the thickest breast to check the inside, her grandmother said nothing, only raised one eyebrow at the pinkish seam near the bone.

"Grandma. Is that done?"

"It's not raw," her grandmother said, which was not the same as yes.

The front door opened early, before her mother, before the rice was ready. It was her father, holding a bakery bag in one hand and a narrow plastic case in the other. He set the bag down and held up the case like a man presenting evidence. "You're not going to guess at it," he said. "US food safety agencies say chicken is safely cooked when its internal temperature hits 165 degrees Fahrenheit. That's about 74 degrees Celsius. You measure it with a food thermometer." He unsnapped the case and handed her the probe, thin as a knitting needle, and she took it wondering how long he'd had it in the car, whether he'd bought it today on some errand he hadn't mentioned.

"It's fine," she said. "I've done this before."

"You've cut it open before. That's not the same thing." He said it mildly, and she could hear the argument underneath, the one they'd been circling since she'd announced she wanted to take a gap year: that her methods were improvised, that improvisation was another word for risk. She slid the probe into the thickest part of the breast, angling toward the center the way the little diagram on the case showed, and watched the digital numbers climb and settle. 161.

"Close," her father said.

"So two more minutes," Ashley said, and pulled the probe out and slid the pan back in, and found she was oddly pleased, as though the number had taken a side in the argument and it wasn't his.

While the oven ticked, her grandmother asked what she was reading, and Ashley told her about a philosophy module from the online course she'd started, the free one, the one her father called a distraction. "It's about determinism," she said. "The idea that everything you do was already set in motion before you did it. Every choice is just the last domino." She wiped down the counter. "The chicken's a good example. If the oven runs hot and the pan's on the left and I turn it at four-thirty, the temperature isn't random. It was always going to be what it is."

"Or you could have turned it at five," her grandmother said, "and then it would be something else. What you do still counts."

"That's the whole fight, actually," Ashley said. "Whether the domino knows it's a domino."

Her father snorted from the doorway, and she could tell he wanted to say that a domino that thinks it's free is still a domino, but he held it, and she was grateful, and she thought about how much of their disagreements were ancillary anyway, the gap year, the course, the plan, all of it orbiting the one question neither of them asked directly, which was whether she could be trusted to build her own life without supervision.

At two minutes she tested again. The probe settled at 167, and she showed her father the display, and he nodded once, and that single nod carried more than his whole speech would have. She let the chicken rest while she finished the rice and the salad her grandmother had insisted was ancillary, which made Ashley laugh, because the old woman had used the same word a different way and could not have known it.

At dinner, with her mother finally there and the candles lit because her grandmother believed in candles for any occasion that survived, her father cut into his chicken and paused. "This is the best thing you've made," he said, and her grandmother said, "The parsley's too fine," and everyone talked over each other about whether parsley could be too fine, and Ashley sat back and ate and let the noise of it wash around her, still not sure whether she'd chosen any of it or merely followed a chain that began in a hot oven and ended here, and finding she didn't much mind the not knowing. Later, washing up, she dried the thermometer probe with a towel and slid it back into its case, and set it on the windowsill where the morning light would find it.

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The word valedictorian comes from the Latin vale dicere, meaning "to say farewell," which is why the valedictorian gives a farewell speech.
story:
The speech was due to Mr. Tse by five o'clock and Maika had written, crossed out, and rewritten the first line eleven times in the back seat of her mother's car, which was parked at the edge of the school lot with the windows cracked because June had begun to metastasize across every surface, the asphalt, the hood, the steering wheel. "Good morning, we are gathered here" was dead on arrival. "As I stand before you" was worse, a phrase worn smooth by strangers. Her mother had gone inside to find the gym teacher about the caps, which had been ordered in the wrong colour, so Maika had the car and the lot and her own restlessness to herself, at least until Jeremie rapped two knuckles on the glass.

"Valedictorian," he said, sliding into the passenger seat with the ceremony program folded in his back pocket. "You realize you haven't written it yet. Lucia told me. She said you were in the library yesterday staring at a blank document like it owed you money."

"It does owe me money." She turned the notebook toward him so he could witness the carnage. Every page had one sentence and a thick black line through it. "The problem is goodbye. Every way of saying it sounds like a greeting card. Like someone ironed the feeling flat and laminated it."

Jeremie read the crossed-out lines with the solemnity of a customs officer. "Some of these are genuinely terrible," he said, with affection. "This one, though, 'we were all allotropes of the same element,' that's not bad. Chemistry class metastasizing into the graduation speech."

"It's carbon," Maika said. "Diamond and graphite. Same element, different arrangement. It's a real thing, it's precise, and it still means something about people. But it doesn't solve goodbye." She dropped the notebook on the dash. "That's the whole job, apparently. Say farewell to two hundred people you've known since you were twelve, in four minutes, without sounding corny. That's the assignment. Nobody teaches you the part that's actually hard."

Jeremie frowned at the visor for a while, the way he did when a math problem was rearranging itself behind his eyes. Then he sat up. "Wait. Do you know where the word even comes from? Valedictorian. I found it in the Latin club notes when I was cleaning out my locker. Vale dicere. It means 'to say farewell.' That's why the valedictorian gives a farewell speech. The whole title is just the job description. You're not giving a speech and also saying goodbye. The saying goodbye is the speech."

Maika looked at him, then out at the lot, where a groundskeeper was dragging a hose toward the flowerbeds by the flagpole and the water caught the light in brief arcs. "So it's not two problems," she said slowly. "It's one. The word isn't a rank with a speech attached. The word is the farewell." She was quiet, and then she laughed, surprising herself. "I've been trying to bolt a goodbye onto a speech like a spoiler on a car. When the goodbye is the engine."

"That's a terrible metaphor," Jeremie said, "and I understand it completely."

She took up the pen and wrote across the top of a fresh page, and the words came faster than she could have predicted, though she was honest enough, watching them appear, to know she couldn't yet tell whether they were true or merely felt true, whether the speech would hold or whether some specious prettiness had slipped in disguised as insight. That was the trouble with her own writing: she could audit everyone else's. She would have to read it aloud to find out, the way you test a bridge by walking on it. "Okay," she said, gathering the pages. "I need a listener. Neutral. Unimpressed."

"Lucia's by the gym doors," Jeremie said, already out of the car. "She claims she'll cry at anything today, so she's the opposite of neutral, but she's sitting in the shade."

They crossed the lot together, the asphalt giving back heat in waves, and Maika ran the lines once under her breath, vale dicere, to say farewell, and thought how strange and convenient it was that a school had handed her a word that was also an instruction. Lucia looked up from the step, saw the notebook, and put down her phone. "Read it to me," she said. "But if you say 'journey,' I'm leaving."

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: Gillian Flynn's 2012 novel Gone Girl alternates between two narrators, and one of them, Amy, is revealed to have written a false diary to mislead the police.
story:
Brayden caught the 7:14 bus with the novel still open in his hand, his thumb holding the page like a bookmark, though he had stopped reading two stops ago. Nour slid into the seat across the aisle and knocked her knuckles against his knee.

"Don't tell me you finished it."

"Last night. Three in the morning." He closed the book on his finger. "You're at the diary part?"

"I'm at the part where I feel like garbage for believing every word she wrote." Nour pulled her own copy out of her bag, its cover soft from being bent backward. "Kai's calling it a betrayal. He says Flynn cheated."

"That's what I thought too, at first."

Kai leaned over the seat in front of them, earbuds hanging around his neck. "You're defending her? You were the one who said the diary chapters were the most honest writing you'd ever read."

Brayden looked down at the book. Gone Girl, with its cracked spine and the library sticker going grey at the corner. He had said that. He had underlined two of Amy's diary entries in pencil, small careful marks, because the loneliness in them had felt true.

"Okay, so here's the thing," he said. "The book alternates. Two narrators. Nick's chapters, then Amy's diary, back and forth, all the way to the middle. And then it turns out the diary is fake. She wrote it to mislead the police. She planted it."

Kai frowned. "The whole thing?"

"The whole thing. Every entry we trusted." Brayden turned the book over in his hands. "So Kai's question is fair. Did she trick us, or did she show us how a trick works?"

The bus lurched around the corner by the pharmacy and Nour grabbed the pole. "That's the part I can't figure out. I trusted the diary more than I trusted Nick. He was lying about where he was, he was hiding things, and she seemed, I don't know, open."

"Exactly." Brayden felt something assembling itself as he spoke, the way a proof does on a whiteboard, each line making the next one possible. "That's not an accident. Flynn made the liar seem unreliable and the liar seem honest, and we fell for it because we read the diary the way we read diaries. Like it's private. Like nobody writes a diary to be read by police."

Kai sat back down, then popped up again, chin on the seat. "So the point of view itself is the weapon."

"That might be too far," Brayden said. "But it's close." He had learned this word in Ms. Mercado's class on Tuesday, leitmotif, a returning phrase that gathers meaning each time it comes back, and he thought the diary worked like that, each entry a small refrain that kept promising sincerity until the promise collapsed. "Here's what I keep going back and forth on, though. If the diary is fake, then the woman who wrote the fake diary is the real Amy. So in a weird way the diary is honest. It's an honest portrait of dishonesty."

Nour made a face. "That's the kind of thing Ms. Mercado would put on a test."

"She'd put it on a test and then take points off for hedging," Brayden said, and Kai laughed.

The bus slowed for the school turn. Brayden thought about the small underground current he'd sensed on his second read, that subterranean wrongness in Amy's early entries, the sentences that were a little too perfect, a little too composed for a woman who was supposed to be afraid. He had missed it the first time because he wanted to miss it. He had wanted the diary to be true.

"I still don't know if that makes it a good book or a cruel one," he said, standing as the bus hissed into its bay. "I believe both, some days. Ask me after the discussion."

They filed down the steps. Ms. Mercado was standing at the door of the school with her clipboard, taking attendance for the field trip that wasn't, the one nobody had told Brayden had been cancelled, which meant his class would spend first period in the gym watching a safety video instead of debating the novel at all.

Kai clapped him on the shoulder. "Guess we'll never know what you'd have said."

"Ask me on the bus home," Brayden said, and held the door open for Nour, diary still warm in his bag, fake and true at once.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A journal's impact factor, devised by Eugene Garfield, is the average number of citations received in one year by articles the journal published in the previous two years.
story:
Phoenix spread the two articles across Olivia's kitchen table like cards in a trick, tapping the one printed on heavier stock. "This one wins before you start. Its journal has an impact factor of nine," she said. "The other one's in some journal I've never heard of."

Olivia's mother had left a plate of sliced apples between the two papers, which felt, somehow, like diplomacy. Dana pulled her chair closer and read the first page of each article without touching either, the way you look at two dogs you don't yet trust.

"You don't even know what the number means," Olivia said.

"It means better. Everyone knows that."

But Olivia didn't, and the not-knowing had been itching at her since Ms. Oyelaran handed out the assignment on Tuesday: a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question, and not a summary, an argument. Olivia had chosen two pieces about whether homework improved achievement, one from the glossy journal, one from the obscure one, because they disagreed completely and she could not yet say which one was wrong. She had been calling herself an autodidact since seventh grade, mostly as a joke, but this was the first time the self-teaching had felt like standing at the bottom of something tall.

"Do we have to pick a winner?" Dana asked, quiet, eyes still on the page. "Because my brother says the whole point of college is learning to hold two things at once."

Phoenix's shoulders came up around her ears. Olivia had seen that before, in eighth grade, when Phoenix won the regional math prize and then spent a week certain everyone was waiting for her to lose it. The bragging was not arrogance, or not only; it was a congenital flinch dressed up as confidence, and Olivia had learned to answer the flinch, not the boast.

Later, when Dana and Phoenix had gone home and the apples had browned, Olivia sat cross-legged on her bed with her laptop and typed the phrase into the search bar. She found Eugene Garfield's name first, then the definition, and read it three times. A journal's impact factor was the average number of citations received in one year by articles the journal had published in the previous two years. She copied it onto an index card, then read it aloud to her ceiling, then once more slowly, letting each phrase settle. Average. Citations. One year. Previous two years.

Phoenix, at home across town, lay on her own bed rereading the rejection email from the summer program, the one that said applicants were evaluated holistically, and understood from the word holistic that she had lost to something she couldn't see and couldn't parametrize into a formula she could beat next time. Numbers had always been her shelter. Nine was bigger than two; that was the whole of her argument, and she knew, lying there, that it was thin, and that Olivia had looked at her tonight the way people look at you when they've caught the seam showing.

The next afternoon Phoenix came back without being invited, standing in the doorway of Olivia's kitchen with the obscure article rolled in her fist. "Okay," she said. "Tell me the thing."

Olivia set down the index card beside the apples, which her mother had refreshed, because her mother noticed things like that. "So the impact factor," she said, and pushed the card across. "It counts citations. That's all it counts."

Phoenix read it. Her mouth moved slightly on average number of citations, and Olivia watched her do the arithmetic of her own error, the visible recalculation. "So a journal could be old and big and get cited a lot for one famous paper," Phoenix said slowly, "and that says nothing about this article, or the methods, or whether the statistics are any good."

"It says people talk about it. Talking isn't the same as being right." Olivia slid the second article toward her. "I still can't tell which one's right. The small journal's study is better designed, I think, but it's on fewer students, and the big journal's author replies to almost every criticism like she's fencing. I might end up saying neither one closes it."

Dana, who had arrived halfway through and was eating an apple slice at the counter, pointed the core at both of them. "So the review is you, standing between them, saying what you'd need to see."

The light went long and orange across the table. Phoenix unrolled the obscure article, smoothed it flat with both palms, and found a pencil in her bag.

"Start with the sample size," she said. "I'll do the math."

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Subtext is the meaning beneath what characters actually say, such as anger or love that a line never names out loud.
story:
Ms. Rivera had pushed the desks to the walls of Room 114 and taped a rectangle of masking tape to the floor, and Maika stood at the edge of it holding her script like something that might go off in her hands. "Ten minutes," Ms. Rivera said. "One moment from your own life. That's the whole assignment." Juan was already sprawled in a folding chair with his feet on a stack of dictionaries, reading his draft with the particular ennui of someone who has written six pages and believes in none of them.

Maika's play was about the night her mother sold the piano. It had sat in the corner of the living room since before Maika could talk, and one Tuesday in eighth grade two men came with a dolly and took it away, and her mother had said, "We need the space," and Maika had said, "Fine, whatever," and gone to her room. That was the scene. She had written it exactly as it happened, four lines of dialogue and a stage direction that said the men carry the piano out. When she read it aloud to Juan and Katelyn, Juan looked up and said, "That's it? Nobody says anything."

"It's what happened," Maika said. "She said we needed the space and I said fine."

Katelyn turned her own script over and leaned forward. "Okay, but my piece is about the fight I had with my brother, and the first draft was just us screaming our actual feelings at each other, and it was terrible. Like a journal entry with chairs." She tapped Juan's pages. "Yours too. You made your dad literally announce that he was disappointed in you. Nobody does that."

Juan sat up a little. "Then what do they do?"

"They say something else." Katelyn pulled up her second draft and held it out. In the new version, the siblings argued about whose turn it was to unload the dishwasher, and neither one mentioned the thing they were actually furious about, which was that he had read her texts and she had told their mother about his girlfriend. Maika read it twice. The dishwasher fight was somehow worse, in the good way; it made her chest hurt. "The fight on the page isn't the real fight," she said slowly. "The real one's underneath."

"That's the subtext," Katelyn said. "The meaning under what they actually say. Like anger or love that the line never names out loud."

Ms. Rivera drifted past their corner long enough to hear Katelyn's second read-through, and said only, "Better," before moving on to torment the boys near the window, which Maika found more useful than any speech. She sat on the floor inside the taped rectangle with her script and thought about her mother saying they needed the space. Her mother had said it while wiping the spot on the floor where the piano leg had been, and Maika had said fine while standing in the doorway with her music folder still in her hand. She had assumed, in four years of occasionally thinking about it, that her mother had wanted the money. It had not occurred to her until now that there might be something underneath the words her mother chose, some meaning that never got named, and that she herself had done the same thing with fine, whatever, which had not been fine and had not been whatever.

She rewrote the scene right there on the floor. Now the mother said, "You can practice at school, they have rooms," and the daughter said, "I wasn't going to practice anyway," and neither of them looked at the empty corner. It was truer and harder to look at, and she understood she was guessing. She could not actually know what her mother had meant; she was writing a version, the way Katelyn's brother would probably deny that the dishwasher fight was ever about the texts. Ms. Rivera was always saying that a play problematizes memory, that autobiography is a construction, and Maika had rolled her eyes at the word, but sitting inside the tape rectangle she felt the truth of it. She could only build one possible mother and put her on the stage.

Katelyn, who could be annoyingly perspicacious about other people's business, read the new pages over her shoulder and said, "This one's yours." Juan volunteered to play the mother, standing with his knees together and his voice pitched up, and it should have been funny but it wasn't; when he said, "They have rooms at school," the room got quiet and even the boys by the window stopped talking. Maika watched from the folding chair where the daughter would sit. She still didn't know if she would ever ask her mother the real question, whether the piano was money or grief or something with no name at all. But she had made a door in the floor of it, and she knew now that a door was different from an answer.

"Take it from the top," she said. "And this time, don't look at the corner."

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: Putting another writer's idea into your own words still requires a citation, because plagiarism covers using ideas without credit, not only copying exact wording.
story:
Hudson had written the whole thing in one sitting, which he knew was the problem, but it was also eleven at night and the paper was due at eight in the morning. The assignment sheet from Ms. Tran said the paper needed an argument, at least six sources, footnotes, and a bibliography in Chicago style, whatever distinctions Chicago wanted to draw between a footnote and a bibliography at that hour. He had an argument, sort of, about how the city's redesign of the riverfront had pushed out the fishermen who had used the docks for decades. He had sources. What he did not have was patience, so when he found a paragraph in a city-planning journal that said exactly what he wanted to say, he retyped it in his own words, changing "municipal priorities" to "what the city cared about" and feeling, briefly, like a translator rather than a thief. He left the page number out of his notes because he didn't think he'd need it.

The next morning Ms. Tran returned drafts with one word stamped in green ink at the top of each. His said REVISION. He found Katia and Umar at the long table by the windows, Katia turning her own draft over so nobody could read the red scrawl across it, Umar stacking his footnotes like cards, each one a small monument to a night he clearly regretted.

"You reworded something," Ms. Tran said when Hudson reached her desk. She had his paper open to the third page, where the riverfront paragraph sat, plump and fluent in a way the rest of the paper was not. "There's no note here."

"I put it in my own words," Hudson said. "It's mine now."

She looked at him for a long moment, then closed the paper and slid it back. "Read the handbook, page forty. Then come tell me what you find. I'm not going to fight you for it." She said it without sharpness, the way she said most things, as though the argument were already over and she was simply waiting for him to catch up.

He sat back down across from Umar, who pushed half his sandwich toward him without being asked, having watched Hudson skip breakfast often enough to know the signs. Hudson ate and opened the handbook to page forty, where a single sentence had been underlined by some student in a previous year, in pencil so faint it adumbrated the point more than it made it: putting another writer's idea into your own words still requires a citation, because plagiarism covers using ideas without credit, not only copying exact wording.

"So what happened?" Katia asked. She had given up on hiding her draft and was peeling the stamp off with one fingernail.

"I paraphrased a paragraph and figured that meant I didn't have to cite it," Hudson said. "But plagiarism isn't just copying the exact wording. It's using ideas without credit." Saying it out loud made it worse, somehow, and also clearer. He could feel the two halves of the thing grinding against each other: the part of him that had genuinely understood the riverfront argument, and the part of him that had let a stranger do the understanding first and then dressed it in his own coat.

Umar leaned over. "Then you cite the paraphrase. Same footnote, same page number. It's actually easier than what you did, all that rewording."

"That's the insulting part," Hudson said. "I worked hard to disguise it. If I'd just quoted it honestly it would've been less work and less wrong."

Katia laughed, then stopped laughing when she looked at her own draft. "I think I did the same thing on page two. The thing about the ferry schedule." She pulled the paper back toward herself and went quiet, scanning.

Hudson spent the period hunting down the journal article again, copying its author, title, page number, the whole munificent apparatus of citation that had seemed like bureaucracy yesterday and looked now like something closer to gratitude. On the back of his draft he wrote a note to himself: even when it sounds like me, if the idea came from someone else, the idea gets a name attached. He was still uncertain about the edges of it, whether an idea could ever really belong to anyone, whether everything he thought had come from somewhere else first. He didn't write that part down. It seemed like a question for the paper's last paragraph, maybe, the kind Ms. Tran would circle and write MORE beside.

At the end of class he brought the revised paragraph up to her desk, footnote attached. She read it, then read the footnote, then looked up.

"Better," she said. "Now tell me why you left the sentence about the fishermen out."

"I couldn't find where I got it."

"Then find out," she said, "or find out it was yours."

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: The '10 percent rule', never raising weekly running distance more than 10 percent, is a popular guideline, but studies have not shown it prevents injuries better than other gradual plans.
story:
Coralie taped the grid to the inside of her locker door, six columns wide, one for each day of the season. Monday easy four kilometres, Wednesday intervals, Saturday long run, Sunday nothing at all. The math had taken her most of Sunday evening, because she was building it on a law she'd learned from Mr. Nielsen in the first week: never raise your weekly distance by more than 10 percent. Thirty-five kilometres this week meant at most thirty-eight and a half the next. She liked how the rule converted ambition into arithmetic, how it made the season look like a staircase instead of a cliff.

"You're smiling at a spreadsheet," Gracie said, leaning against the neighbouring locker. "That's genuinely concerning."

"It's a training program. Real runners have them. Seerat's cousin had one and she made regionals."

"Seerat's cousin also stress-fractured her shin," Gracie said. "Just saying."

At the track that afternoon, Coralie ran her easy four with the paper folded in her pocket, and afterwards she sat on the infield grass with Seerat, cross-checking her weeks against a phone calculator. Seerat was the one who found it. She'd been searching for a better warm-up routine when a study summary surfaced on her screen, and she read it twice, frowning, before she turned the phone so Coralie could see.

"Wait," Seerat said. "It says the 10 percent rule is popular, but studies haven't shown it prevents injuries any better than other gradual plans."

Coralie took the phone. She read the line three times, as if the words might rearrange themselves into something she could keep. "That can't be right. Mr. Nielsen said..."

"He said what he was taught, probably." Seerat shrugged. "Everybody says it. That doesn't make it evidence."

Gracie, who had finished her strides and come over to sprawl in the grass, watched Coralie's face do something complicated. From where Gracie sat, the whole thing looked almost funny: Coralie had spent a weekend worshipping a number, and now the number had turned out to be more of a folk belief than a law. But Gracie had also watched Coralie run herself into the ground last season, had literally carried her water bottle on the day she could barely walk, and she understood what Coralie was actually afraid of. Not the loss of the rule. The loss of the guarantee.

"So the rule doesn't protect me," Coralie said slowly. "But the studies don't say gradual is bad, either. They say other gradual plans work about the same."

"Correct," Seerat said.

"Then the staircase is still a staircase. It's just not the only staircase." Coralie unfolded her paper and looked at it differently now, less like a contract and more like a draft. "I still want rest days. I still want warm-ups before intervals. I'm just not going to treat point five of a kilometre like it's going to incapacitate me."

"You were never going to be incapacitated by half a kilometre," Gracie said. "You might be incapacitated by your own brain, though."

They walked to the fence together as the light went long and orange across lane eight. Coralie kept thinking of her father, who fixed cars and distrusted any rule he couldn't test. The 10 percent rule had become, for her, a kind of synecdoche, the one part standing for the whole business of coaching, and now the part had cracked. She didn't know yet what to put in its place. Maybe nothing. Maybe judgment, which was harder than arithmetic and had no grid.

The next morning she found Mr. Nielsen in the equipment shed, counting cones. "I read about the 10 percent rule," she said. "That it's a guideline, and studies haven't shown it works better than other gradual plans."

He set down a cone and looked at her for a long moment, then laughed, not unkindly. "Where did you find that?"

"On my own. So I'm keeping the plan, but I'm changing week six. If I feel good, I'll go up a bit more than ten percent. If I'm tired, less."

"That," Mr. Nielsen said, "is called coaching."

She ran the easy loop that evening without the paper in her pocket, only a rest day circled on her hand in blue ink, one small square she trusted completely, and at the top of the hill she stopped, breathing hard, and looked back at the track emptying in the dusk.

"Tomorrow," she said out loud to nobody, "I rest."

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Dramatic irony is when the audience knows something that a character on stage does not, which lets a short scene build tension quickly.
story:
Hannah moved the coffee table to the wall and set two folding chairs in the middle of the living room, facing each other at an angle, the way she had seen it done in the black box theatre on the field trip in October. The carpet held the marks of the table legs like a fossil record of every ordinary evening that had happened there before this one. On the mantel she propped a single white envelope, angled so that anyone sitting in the kitchen doorway, where the audience would be, could read the words she had written across it in her mother's handwriting, copied letter by letter: Notification of Transfer, El Paso.

Ismael arrived at four with a bag of chips and the handout from Mr. Nowak's class folded into quarters in his back pocket. He read the first page of her script standing up, then read it again sitting in one of the folding chairs. He was playing her father, which was a strange thing to ask of someone who laughed at his own jokes before he finished them, but he had said yes without hesitating, and she had not thanked him properly for that.

"The whole first minute is just them passing the potatoes," he said. "Is that on purpose?"

"Keep reading."

He kept reading. When he reached the stage direction at the top of page two, he looked up at the envelope on the mantel, then back at her, and she watched the understanding move across his face the way weather moves across a field. "The mom takes the El Paso job before the dad even knows she was offered it," he said slowly. "And we've already seen the envelope. We know she's leaving before the dinner even starts."

"That's dramatic irony," Hannah said. "The audience knows something a character on stage doesn't. I found it in the handout Tuesday night and I rewrote everything after." She had found it, in fact, by accident, reading ahead while her mother watched a cooking show three feet away, and she had sat very still for a long time afterward, because the handout was describing her own living room. Her mother had put the real envelope in the junk drawer six weeks ago, under the batteries, and Hannah had found it looking for tape.

They ran the scene. Ismael held a bowl of imaginary potatoes and asked, in a voice rougher than his own, how her day had been, and Hannah, playing herself, or a version of herself who said the things the real one had not, talked about a chemistry test while the envelope sat over her shoulder like a third person at the table. Twice she broke off because the words refused to sit in her mouth. The scene wanted her mother to say the truth in the last thirty seconds, and her mother had not said it yet in real life. The transfer date was the ninth of June. Nobody in the house had mentioned the ninth of June out loud, not once, as though silence could transmute the fact into something equivocal, something that might still go either way.

There was a knock, and Mr. Nowak from next door stood in the doorway holding the two wooden chairs Hannah's mother had promised he could lend. He set them down inside, watched Ismael and Hannah positioned stiffly in their folding chairs for a moment, and said only, "Nice sightlines," before letting himself back out. Hannah arranged the wooden chairs at the back as an impromptu audience and sat in one, and from there the envelope was perfectly legible, and the two people at the dinner table looked small and doomed and comic all at once.

She understood then that the play was not exactly fair. It gave the audience the mother's secret and let the daughter be innocent of it, when in truth Hannah had known for six weeks and had said nothing, had eaten the dinners and passed the potatoes and hoarded the knowledge like a debt. If she staged the scene honestly, the audience would watch the girl keep the secret too, would watch everyone at the table circling the one fact that no one would say, and the irony would belong to the audience alone, and the family on stage would all be pretending, together, at the same empty ritual. It would be a better play. It would also be a colder one, and she would have to perform her own silence in front of her mother on Thursday night, in the school cafeteria, with the whole class watching.

Ismael ran the scene again from the top. This time, when the father asked how her day had been, Hannah let her eyes flick to the mantel for half a second before she answered, and Ismael caught it and gave her a look that asked whether that was new, and she nodded once. He set down the imaginary bowl.

"Again," he said, and reset his chair with a scrape against the carpet.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: A population pyramid conventionally shows males on the left and females on the right, with age groups stacked from youngest at the bottom to oldest at the top.
story:
The travel agency sat between a dry cleaner and a shuttered phone repair shop, and for three days Julia had been its entire staff, since Ms. Kaur flew to Toronto for her niece's wedding and left a ring of keys and a list of tasks that included "sort the country profiles." The profiles were laminated sheets, one per nation, each with a small chart of stacked bars shaped like a Christmas tree or a barrel or, in the case of Japan, a light bulb. Julia had taken the job because tuition deposits do not pay themselves, and because her aunt knew Ms. Kaur, and because eight dollars above minimum wage for sitting in air conditioning felt like a small fraud she was willing to commit.

She was flipping through the charts on Thursday morning when the bell over the door rang and Yuvraj came in, ostensibly to buy a bus ticket to his cousin's in Detroit, though the bus station sold those for six dollars less. He dropped into the chair across the desk, watched her slide a profile of Nigeria across the desk, and squinted at it. "Is that a graph or a butterfly that lost a fight?"

"It's a population pyramid," Julia said, though until that sentence she had only half believed it. "Ms. Kaur's file says so. I'm supposed to tag each country for the school trip market or the retiree market." She tapped the wide base of Nigeria's chart. "So this bottom part, that's the oldest people, right? Because you put the elders on top normally, but this one's inverted for, I don't know, reasons. Design reasons."

Yuvraj leaned in, turned the sheet sideways as if the problem were one of orientation in the ordinary sense, and then turned it back. "Bottom says zero to four," he read. "So the youngest are at the bottom. And it says male on one side and female on the other." He paused with the particular dignity of someone who has just caught a friend in an error. "Which side is male? Because you said, what, the left was female?"

"I didn't say that," Julia said, and then checked her memory and found that she absolutely had, out loud, twice. The chart's tiny label sat under the left half of the bars. "Males on the left. Females on the right. Youngest at the bottom, oldest at the top." She said it slowly, the way she repeated physics formulas before they dissolved. "So I've been reading every single one of these like a mirror."

"Congratulations," Yuvraj said. "You've discovered that you can't read." He bought the bus ticket anyway, at full price, which she suspected was charity dressed as laziness, and he took two of the peppermints from the bowl by the register, which was definitely theft dressed as friendship.

The problem revealed itself fully at noon, when a woman came in wanting to price a two-year stay in Portugal for her and her husband, and asked, in the offhand way people ask about weather, whether the town they'd chosen online had good hospitals and other "people our age." Julia, who an hour earlier had confidently labeled Portugal's chart retiree-heavy based on her mirrored reading, now held the profile under the desk lamp like a suspect. The sides were close to symmetric, which was the trouble; the real information lived in the bulge near the middle and the narrowing toward the bottom, and she could no longer remember which of her conclusions had been made before the mirror revelation and which after. She quoted the woman a price for travel insurance and said she'd email by Friday with neighborhoods, and the woman left a phone number on a card that smelled faintly of lavender.

Julia texted Cynthia, who was taking an online stats course and responded within minutes with the smug efficiency of someone studying at a pool. "It's just age structure," Cynthia typed. "Young countries, bottom-heavy, think schools. Old countries, top-heavy, think nursing homes. Don't dichotomize it too hard, though. A country can need both." Then, a second message: "Also don't tell my mother I'm doing homework on vacation." Julia laid the profiles out on the desk in a row, Portugal between Germany and Brazil, and did the reading again with the labels in their true positions, and found that her earlier conclusions flipped for almost half the stack. Ms. Kaur's file tags, in her tidy handwriting, disagreed with Julia's first pass on nine countries and agreed on seven, and Julia could not tell which of the seven were luck.

She started a new sheet. For each country she wrote two lines: what the shape suggested, and what she was unsure of. Portugal she marked "aging but with a bulge moving up, not young," and then, in smaller letters, "depends which years the bars cover, ask Ms. Kaur." It occurred to her that she had spent four days wanting to seem like someone who already knew things, and that the new sheet, with its second column of admissions, was the first thing she'd made here that would actually be useful to somebody.

When Ms. Kaur returned on Saturday, tan and carrying a tin of wedding sweets, she read the sheet standing up, one hand on her suitcase handle. "You've made mistakes," she said.

"Nine of them, probably more," Julia said. "But they're the right mistakes now. The first ones were the wrong mistakes."

Ms. Kaur looked at her for a long moment, then set the tin on the counter and took a lavender-scented card from her pocket, the same kind the Portugal woman had left. "She called. She liked that you didn't pretend. Look at the pyramid again and tell me, in your own reading, top heavy or bottom heavy?" Julia pulled the sheet toward her, and put her finger at the bottom of the bars, where the youngest were.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: A naive narrator, such as Huck in Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, reports events honestly but misunderstands them, so readers see more than the narrator does.
story:
The book club met in the back room of the library on the first Tuesday of the month, and Sebastian arrived early because he had promised himself he would say something this time. He had spent three evenings with Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, annotating with a pencil he kept losing in the couch cushions, and he still did not know what he thought about Huck himself.

Sara-Maude was already there, arranging the folding chairs in a circle with the seriousness of someone setting a table for guests she wanted to impress. She had started the club in September and had chosen every book since, and she wanted, Sebastian had gathered, to be the one who understood them first. Neil came in behind him with the paperback crushed sideways in his jacket pocket, and Mr. Njoroge, who lived two streets over and had retired from teaching English at the high school, took the chair nearest the radiator and waited, as he always did, for someone else to begin.

"Everyone finished?" Sara-Maude asked. Three heads nodded, Neil's a beat late. "Good, because I want to start with the feud chapter. The Grangerfords and the Shepherdsons. It's the funniest thing in the book and I can't explain why."

Neil demurred. "It's not funny. A whole family gets shot in a river."

"It is funny," Sara-Maude said. "You laughed. I heard you."

"I laughed at the part where Buck can't spell Moses."

Sebastian turned to his notes, which were less notes than arguments with himself. He had underlined the moment when Huck, watching the feud's violence unfold, says only that it was tough to see, and then worries about a pig. He had written in the margin, twice, the same question: does Huck know what he's telling us? He had first thought the answer was no, then thought it was yes, and had circled the word yes and then crossed the circle out.

"Here's my problem," he said, and the room went quiet in the way that made his ears warm. "Huck describes the feud like he's describing weather. He tells us everything and understands none of it. When the church sermon is about brotherly love and everybody says it was a good sermon while they're carrying guns in, Huck just reports it and moves on. He doesn't get the joke. So who's making the joke?"

"Twain," Neil said.

"Then Huck isn't unreliable," Sebastian said. "He's telling the truth the whole way through. He never lies to us about what happened. He lies to himself about what it means." He looked at the margin of his book, where he had crossed out his own certainty. "I had it backwards for most of the week. I kept trying to find where Huck deceives us, and there isn't a where."

Mr. Njoroge shifted his chair an inch. "There's a name for that kind of narrator," he said, and stopped, because he had a rule about not doing the work.

Sara-Maude found it first, flipping through the introduction she had skipped. "A naive narrator," she read. "Reports events honestly but misunderstands them." She looked up. "So we see more than he does. That's why the feud is funny and horrible at the same time. We're standing behind him, seeing past his shoulder."

Sebastian felt the two halves of his week come together, the suspicion of lying and the absence of lies, and settle into something he could actually hold. Huck was honest and mistaken, and the mistake was the point. "That's why the funny scenes work," he said. "The circus scene. Huck thinks the drunk who gets on the horse is really a drunk, and we know he's a performer, and Huck's worry is funnier than any joke about drunks would be. Twain can't say anything directly because Huck would have to understand it, and Huck can't understand it or the whole book collapses."

"So it's a trick," Neil said. "Twain gets to be grandiose about slavery and conscience without ever raising his voice. He puts all the sermonizing into a kid who thinks he's going to hell for helping Jim."

"It's not a trick if it's the whole architecture," Sara-Maude said, and Neil opened his mouth, and for a minute they went back and forth about whether a writer who hides that thoroughly is being honest or cowardly, Neil maintaining that irony was a kind of insurance, Sara-Maude that it was fiduciary in spirit, that Twain had taken on the reader's trust and had to account for every page of it. Sebastian listened without taking a side, because the part he was sure of was narrower than either of theirs.

What he was sure of: the narration worked, and it worked by withholding understanding rather than withholding facts. What he was not sure of: whether Huck stays naive at the end, after the bit with Jim and the raft, or whether Twain simply needed him to become naive again to land the closing chapters, and the book broke something in order to finish. He said so, the uncertainty included, and Mr. Njoroge nodded once, which meant more from him than a paragraph of praise.

Sara-Maude was already writing the next book on the little whiteboard, and she turned before capping the marker. "You're leading next month, then. You clearly have the method down."

"I have half of it down," Sebastian said. "The other half I got wrong for five days."

Mr. Njoroge pulled on his coat. "That's usually how you can tell you've learned something," he said, and then, before Sebastian could decide whether that was a lesson, he picked up Huck's crushed paperback from the table, smoothed the cover flat with the heel of his hand, and handed it back to Neil.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Cheating out means an actor turns their body partly toward the audience, even while talking to another character, so their face and voice carry.
story:
The living room had been a living room until Tuesday, when Luca pushed the couch against the window and taped a rectangle of masking tape on the floorboards for the stage. Now it held a folding card table with his script binder, a mug of cold coffee, and a director's chair his mother had bought as a joke, which he used anyway because the joke had become a thing he needed. The one-act was his to run. Mr. Warsame had handed it over with the flat confidence of a man who had watched too many students fail to argue with him, and Luca had discovered, walking home, that being trusted felt like being dropped into deep water.

Haley played the sister, and Gary played the brother, and the play was mostly the two of them arguing in a kitchen about whether their father had been a good man. Luca had picked it for that argument, for the way it refused to settle. On the first evening of real blocking, he set them facing each other, Haley by the fireplace that stood in for the stove, Gary by the armchair that stood in for the table, and he walked around them once, twice, then sat on the floor where the imaginary audience would be.

From there he could see Haley's face and the back of Gary's head. Only the back. Gary's whole performance, the drops in his voice, the way his jaw set before the cruel lines, was aimed at the mantelpiece clock. "You're losing him," Luca said, and Gary turned, and Haley said, "Now I'm losing you," and they stood in the middle of the room like two people waiting for a bus that had already gone by.

Luca tried to fix it with furniture. He rotated the armchair, angled the tape rectangle, dragged the coffee table into the hall until his mother asked from the kitchen if the table had done something wrong. Nothing worked for longer than a page, because the scene required them to face each other, and an audience, wherever Luca sat, was always a third person the actors kept forgetting existed.

It was Haley who came in the next evening with the answer, or half of it, relayed from her cousin who did summer theater. "She kept saying this word. Cheating out." Luca wrote it in the margin of the script without understanding it, and Gary, stretching on the rug, said, "Sounds like a card game." It was at the third rehearsal, when Luca got up to show Gary where to stand and found himself half-turned, talking to Gary while his own body pointed toward the empty armchair where the audience lived, that the thing came clear. Cheating out meant turning partly toward the audience even while you talked to another character, so your face and voice carried past your scene partner and out into the dark.

He made them do it. It looked wrong from inside the scene, staged and unnatural, both actors quartered away from each other like compass needles that couldn't agree on north. But when Luca sat on the floor again, at audience level, the scene opened up the way a window does when a latch lifts. He could see Gary's face during the confession. He could see Haley register it. "That's it," Luca said. "Don't look right at each other. Look mostly, mostly at each other, and give the rest of you to the chairs."

They ran the scene and it found a rhythm, and Luca began to understand that directing was not the virulent kind of control he had feared, the kind his old coach used, barking until the field smelled of obedience. It was closer to hosting. His notes got smaller. He stopped saying "make it bigger" and started saying "let me see you decide." When Gary asked whether the father had been lying in the second monologue, Luca said, "I honestly don't know. Play it like you don't either," and Gary did, and the not-knowing was better than any answer would have been.

Still, the question of the ending sat with him on the drive home and then in his own living room, where he lay on the couch and stared at the ceiling. The play argued that a bad man could still be a loved one, and Luca believed that and didn't believe it, the way he believed and didn't believe things about his grandfather, whose funeral had been in March and whose stories were already changing shape in the family's mouths. He had wanted the play to settle something for him. It refused, which was either its failure or its honesty. He couldn't tell yet, and Mr. Warsame, when Luca asked him after class on Thursday, only said, "Good. That's the question you should still have on opening night." Luca had wanted a verdict and got a permission instead, and he was still deciding whether to be grateful.

The last rehearsal before the move to the stage, Haley brought cookies from a box mix and ate most of them herself, defending the remainder with such flat hedonism that Gary had to buy his way in with a compliment about her second monologue. They ran the play start to finish with no stops, and Luca sat on the floor in the taped rectangle's shadow, watching two people talk to each other and to him at the same time, their bodies half-turned, faces open, voices carrying all the way to the wall.

When it ended, nobody spoke for a second. Then Gary, still half-turned toward the empty chairs, said, "From out there, does it look like we're in a real room?" Luca got up off the floor, crossed to the mantel, and looked back the long way, at the tape rectangle and the two of them inside it, waiting.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: The key signature of G major has one sharp, F-sharp, which applies to every F in the piece unless an accidental changes it.
story:
Zoe had promised Ms. Lindqvist the melody by Friday, and it was Tuesday, and the sixteen bars she had written in the music room after school looked, on the page, like something a real composer might have made. She had chosen G major because it only asked one sharp of her, and she had filled the staves with quarter notes and half notes, a phrase that rose and then folded back on itself the way a question does when you don't want to hear the answer yet.

"That's not a melody, that's a hostage situation," said Maximilian, who had come in to practise timpani and instead kept leaning over her shoulder. "Every note is safe. You land on G every two bars like you're afraid of falling."

"I'm not afraid of falling. I'm afraid of landing somewhere stupid."

"Those are the same thing," said Genevieve from the piano bench, where she was supposed to be drilling scales. She played Zoe's first four bars, plunking them out with one hand, and something was wrong. Zoe heard it before she could name it. The tune arrived at each cadence slightly sideways, like a picture hung a degree off true, and the wrongness was small enough that you might blame the piano, or the room, or your own ears.

"Play it again," Zoe said, and Genevieve did, and Zoe stood very still with her eyes closed. The fourth bar was the worst. She had written an F there, a whole note, meant to be the soft lean before the resolution home, and it came out flat, sour, a door that wouldn't shut. She looked down at the page. At the start of the staff, after the treble clef, sat her key signature: one sharp on the top line. She had drawn it herself, carefully, and then forgotten it entirely.

"Every F in the piece is F-sharp," she said, mostly to herself. "That's the whole point of the key signature. One sharp, and it counts every single time unless I write an accidental to change it." She had known this, in the way you know a fact for a test, and she had not known it at all, in the way that matters. She picked up her pencil. Where the melody used F-sharp, she now had to decide: was the natural sound she wanted in bar four actually a mistake, or was it a choice she had stumbled into? She wrote the sharp sign in front of the note, the little crooked ladder, and Genevieve played it again.

"Better," Genevieve said. "Worse," Maximilian said at the same time, and began to gesticulate at the page with both hands, as if he could physically drag the melody somewhere more interesting. "It's correct now and it's boring now. You fixed the sourness and the sourness was the only part I liked."

Ms. Lindqvist appeared in the doorway with a stack of folders and her irascible expression, the one that meant she had heard everything through the wall and had opinions. She did not offer them. She set the folders down, listened to Genevieve play the sixteen bars twice through, and said only, "Thursday, then. Bring the pencil." Then she was gone, and Zoe sat with the strange doubled feeling of having a page that was right and a page that was alive and no way to tell whether they could be the same page.

She thought of the chemistry unit they had just finished, where the teacher had shown them that carbon could be graphite or diamond, the same element arranged differently, an allotrope, the word itself stiff and formal in her mouth. The notes were the notes either way. What changed was the arrangement, and the arrangement was where the value lived, and she could not shake the suspicion that the natural in bar four was her allotrope, the same melody made of slightly different stuff, and that correcting it might be polishing away the only diamond in the thing.

She erased the accidental she had just added, then wrote it again, then erased it once more, the paper going thin and grey at that spot. Genevieve watched her do this without comment. Maximilian had finally gone to his timpani and was rolling softly on the low drum, a sound like distant weather. Zoe copied the whole melody out fresh on a new sheet, leaving bar four blank, and played the three notes before it and the two notes after it, over and over, listening to the hole where the F should go.

"Pick one," Genevieve said, finally. "It can't be both."

"It might have to be," Zoe said, and set her pencil down against the sharp at the beginning of the staff.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: An ad hominem argument attacks the person making a claim instead of the claim itself, and it is treated as a fallacy in formal debate.
story:
The library at four o'clock held the particular hush of a place being used for something other than its purpose. Tristan had pushed two tables together near the periodicals, and on them he spread his notes: a page of Spanish vocabulary, a page of argument, and between them the gap he had come to close. In nine days he would stand in front of his seminar class and, for five minutes, debate the city's proposal to expropriate land along the riverfront for a light rail line, and he would have to do all of it in Spanish.

He had chosen the topic because the words were easy to learn. Expropiar. Ferrocarril. Impuesto. What he had not counted on was that the argument itself kept slipping away from him whenever he reached for the language. He would begin a sentence about fair compensation for displaced tenants, arrive at the third clause, and find that the Spanish for the third clause had gone quiescent somewhere in his memory, waiting to be woken.

Samira dropped her backpack on the far side of the table and sat down without asking. She was the other half of the exercise, assigned by Mr. Anderson, who had told them only that they would be opponents and that the debate had to survive without translation. She peeled an orange in slow spirals and watched Tristan fail the same sentence twice.

"Otra vez," she said. Again.

"Trenes," Tristan said, "reducen la contaminación, pero el gobierno puede," and then he stopped, because what he wanted was the word for a cost that falls on people who did not choose it. He knew the idea in English, had even written it down: the noise, the shading of gardens, the disruption during construction were externalities, harms borne by the neighbours rather than by the riders or the agency. He could not make the Spanish carry it, so he pointed at his notes and let the page say it.

"Quiero decir," he said slowly, "los costos para los vecinos." The costs for the neighbours. Samira nodded and let it stand, though they both knew that in the real five minutes there would be no notes.

They ran the debate cold, no preparation between turns, and it went badly in the way that mattered. Tristan's Spanish held for the opening and then frayed, and in the fraying he did something he had not planned. Instead of answering Samira's point about compensation rates, he said, "Tu acento es raro," your accent is strange, because she had stumbled on a number and he wanted the floor back. It was a small thing, said almost under his breath, but Samira put down her orange.

"Ad hominem," she said.

"What?"

"That's ad hominem. You attacked me instead of my point." She was not angry; she said it the way someone names a bird they've spotted. "In formal debate it's a fallacy. You lose the exchange." Mr. Anderson, shelving returns three aisles over, did not look up, and Samira did not raise her voice. She simply waited, and Tristan understood that the waiting was the correction.

He sat with it for a moment. He knew the term, or half knew it, from a unit on fallacies in tenth grade, but he had never felt it operate from the inside, from the mouth of the person doing it. It had not felt like a fallacy. It had felt like relief, like a door out of a room where his Spanish was failing him. He tried to imagine the move in English and found he would never have made it there; in English he had arguments enough that he did not need to reach for her instead of her claim.

"Tienes razón," he said. You're right. And then, because a concession without a reply was its own kind of quitting, he bent over his notes and rebuilt the sentence in Spanish, the slower, plainer version. "El gobierno debe pagar más," he said. The government should pay more. Simple, but it answered the thing she had actually said, and Samira shrugged and countered, and for four more exchanges they stayed inside the argument, two people with bad accents and good reasons.

Hunter arrived near five with a bag of chips and the announcement that the riverfront vote had been delayed a month, which meant, Tristan realized, that they were debating a proposal that might change shape before they finished. He could take a position anyway, the plainer position he had found under pressure, and be honest in the last minute about what he could not yet judge: whether fair compensation was even possible, or whether some harms would always land on the neighbours no matter what was paid. He wrote one line at the bottom of his notes and read it aloud to test it, "Hay cosas que no sé todavía," there are things I don't yet know, and Samira picked up another orange and began, unhurried, to peel it.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Canada lowered its federal voting age from 21 to 18 in 1970.
story:
The voter information card arrived on a Tuesday, sandwiched between a pizza flyer and a letter addressed to someone who had moved out before Laurie was born. She carried it into the kitchen and set it on the counter the way she might set down something breakable. Her eighteenth birthday had come and gone in March, quiet, one cake and a phone full of messages, and now here was the proof that the country had noticed too. Elections Canada wanted her at the church hall on Elm Street, doors open at eight-thirty.

"Did you know," she said to her mother that night, "that you couldn't vote at eighteen when you were my age?" Her mother was collating receipts at the table, squaring the corners of each pile against the edge, sorting groceries from gas from the pharmacy. "You'd have been too young. It was twenty-one until 1970. They lowered it to eighteen in 1970, the federal age." She had looked it up that afternoon after finding a thread about it, and the number had stayed with her all evening, the way a song does.

Her mother tapped the receipts flat. "That's the year your uncle was born," she said. "He's never missed a vote in his life. Drives me crazy." She smiled without looking up, which Laurie understood to mean the conversation was welcome but not urgent. Everything in their house was like that, half-attended, and she had spent years deciding whether that was warmth or indifference and had lately settled on the possibility that it was both.

Landyn came over Thursday with his laptop and an energy drink and the confident manner of someone who had read exactly one long article. "It's simple," he said, dropping onto the couch. "If you don't vote, you can't complain. That's the whole social contract." He launched into a scathing riff about people who stay home and then post about the government, and Laurie listened while pretending to scroll, because Landyn was generous and funny and had once driven forty minutes to bring her soup, and none of that made him right about everything.

"Complaining is free, though," she said. "Voting is one afternoon. Do you really think they're the same currency?" Landyn waved this off, but Giovanni, who had arrived halfway through with his shoes still on, said, "She's got you there," and then made it worse by adding that his grandmother had voted in three countries on two continents and considered the ballot a formality compared with what surrounded it. "She says the voting is the easy part," Giovanni said. "The thinking before it, that's the work."

Laurie had been doing the thinking, unevenly.
