She liked one party's climate plan and distrusted its housing numbers; she liked another candidate personally, a local woman named on a flyer she'd kept, and could not reconcile liking her with the party's record. She made a spreadsheet, then abandoned it, then reopened it, because a spreadsheet implied the decision could be optimized and she suspected it could not. There was something she kept circling: that in 1970 someone had decided eighteen-year-olds were finally ready, and she wanted to know what ready was supposed to feel like, because mostly she felt like she was guessing well rather than knowing.

On Saturday she walked to the church hall just to see it, not to vote early, only to stand outside the doors where a volunteer was taping up a sign. Ms. Bighorn, her old grade ten history teacher, was coming out with a coffee. "Laurie," she said. "First time?" Laurie nodded and asked, before she could stop herself, whether it had felt momentous to Ms. Bighorn, the first time. Ms. Bighorn considered this longer than Laurie expected. "I remember the booth being smaller than I thought," she said. "Everything else I've added since." She held the door for an old man with a cane and was gone up the sidewalk.

On Monday evening, Laurie sat at the kitchen table with her marked-up flyer and her half-abandoned spreadsheet and a pen, and her mother set a cup of tea down beside her without comment. Laurie read through her notes one more time, the columns she had made and the places where she had written maybe in the margin instead of an answer. Then she drew a single line under one name, folded the flyer twice, and put it in the pocket of the coat she would wear to the church hall in the morning. The pen rolled off the table and she caught it against her knee.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Acrylic paint is water-based while wet, but it dries quickly and becomes water-resistant once dry.
story:
The community room at the back of the public library smelled like damp cardboard and old coffee, and Paige had claimed the table nearest the window because its light was honest. She was painting a wooden panel for Ms. Dlamini's retirement, a garden of the plants from the courtyard she had tended for nineteen years, and she had promised it would be finished by Saturday. It was Thursday. The acrylics were laid out in shallow trays, thin as puddles after rain, and she worked fast because fast was the only way she knew how to work.

Ally arrived first, dropping her bag on the chair beside Paige's, then Harley, loquacious as always, already halfway through a story about a cashier who had refused his coupon. Paige half-listened. She had learned to let Harley's voice run underneath her painting like radio static, but Ally sat close and quiet and watched the panel, and when Ally spoke it was usually worth hearing.

"You're going hard on the detail," Ally said. "The leaves look like photographs."

"That's the point."

"It looks like homework."

Paige kept her brush moving. The marigolds were going to be exact, every ruffled edge, because Ms. Dlamini knew those flowers by name and Paige wanted her to recognize them the way you recognize a friend across a room. That was one way of loving a person, the precise way. But she could hear something true in what Ally said, that precision could flatten into a report, and she didn't yet know how to hold both ideas at once.

The two of them wanted food. Paige stood, brushed her hands on her jeans, and said five minutes, ten at most, and left her brushes fanned across a paper towel, the good ones, the ones her mother had bought her for her birthday, bristles heavy with orange and green.

They were gone forty minutes. The line at the sandwich place was long, and Harley talked the whole time about his brother, and by the time Paige pushed back through the library's double doors with the paper bag sweating in her hand, she already knew, the way you know before a test is graded. She picked up the first brush and it did not bend. The bristles had set into a stiff, glistening fan, locked at the angle she had left them. She ran the brush under the faucet in the community room's small sink and scrubbed, and the water ran pale orange and then clear and did nothing. The paint had dried to a shell and the shell did not care about water anymore. Wet, it had been hers to move and thin and wash away. Dry, it was permanent, sealed, another material entirely. She stood there metabolizing the fact, her stomach doing the work her mind refused to, and behind her the door opened.

Harley came in with Ally and stopped when he saw the sink. "What happened?"

"I left them out."

"All of them?"

She turned off the faucet. "It's water-based while it's wet. That's why I wasn't careful. But it dries fast, and then it's water-resistant." She said it flatly, not for him, just to hear how stupid it sounded out loud. "So now they're like this."

Harley picked up the smallest brush and tried to flex it with his thumb. "Dead?"

"Maybe not all the way." She had read something once, months ago, a line in a book about materials, and she went to the shelf by the window and found it, a fat handbook on paint. She flipped until the page surrendered itself: the same fact in colder words, with a suggestion after it, a note about loosening hardened acrylic. It might work. It might ruin the brushes further. The book did not promise.

While she worked the bristles with the solvent, Ally sat down in front of the panel and looked at it for a long moment. "You could leave the marigolds the way they are," she said. "Exact. And then do the rest looser. Like the garden from the corner of your eye."

"Then it looks unfinished."

"Then it looks like you were in a hurry to get it all down before it dried on you." Ally shrugged. "Which is what actually happened."

Paige looked at the painting, at the tight golden heads and the untouched space around them, and thought about encapsulation, the way the library had sealed Ms. Dlamini's whole career into a single card in a drawer, and how the card was true and also nothing like the woman. Maybe a painting could be both. Maybe it could keep the marigolds sharp because sharpness was love, and let everything else blur because memory blurred whether you permitted it or not. She didn't know if that was a real decision or an excuse. She picked up the one brush she had revived, the small round one, and held it over the blank part of the panel.

"Sit with me while I ruin it," she said, and Ally pulled her chair around to the window side, and Paige laid the first loose stroke of green down along the bottom of the frame.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Spanish news writers often attribute a claim with 'según', meaning 'according to', which tells a reader the statement comes from a source, not the reporter.
story:
The booth by the window had become their table by unspoken decree, the way things become law when three people repeat them often enough. Laurie spread the newspaper across the ketchup and the napkin dispenser, flattening the crease with the heel of her hand. Her Spanish teacher had assigned each student a short article from a real paper, to be read aloud and summarised from memory on Monday, and Laurie had chosen hers three days late because every article she opened seemed to begin with a sentence of interminable length, clause stacked upon clause like a tower built by someone with no fear of gravity.

"Read it again," Dakota said, stealing a fry. "I like the part where you pronounce every single word like you're apologising to it."

"I'm building confidence."

"You're building a hostage situation."

Maggie leaned over the paper, hair falling into the fries. "What's it about, actually? Beyond the part where you suffered."

Laurie ran her finger under the third sentence. "Something about the water in some town. It says, seg... según el alcalde, el agua es segura. So the water is safe. That's the news. Tap water safe in Valencia or wherever. Fine. Good for them."

"Hold on," Maggie said. "You just read a whole sentence and turned it into a fortune cookie. What does the según part do? Is it like, 'the water is safe, says the mayor'?"

"It's like 'says.' Or 'according to.' Whatever. Same thing."

Dakota lowered the fry with the gravity of a barrister. "It is not the same thing. If the mayor says the water is safe, and the paper says the mayor says the water is safe, those are two different facts. The paper is only promising that the mayor talked."

"That's a very cynical fry," Laurie said, but she looked back at the sentence. Según el alcalde. According to the mayor. The reporter hadn't written el agua es segura on its own, standing naked and responsible in the sentence. The claim was wearing the mayor like a coat. If the water turned out to be full of lead, the reporter had never once said otherwise; the reporter had only passed along what was said, hands clean, attribution in place. She sat back slowly. "Oh no. I've been reading these wrong all week."

The owner, Ms. Chukwu, who had lived next door to Laurie's family since Laurie was six and who ran this place with an iron ladle, chose that moment to interpose a basket of bread between the newspaper and the ketchup. "Books at my tables, fine. Homework at my tables, tolerated. But no crying over Valencia."

"Nobody's crying," Laurie said. "I'm being educated against my will."

Ms. Chukwu tapped the paper once with a flour-dusted finger, on the very word, and said, "según," with the offhand authority of someone saying water is wet. Then she went back to the kitchen, because she was not the kind of adult who stayed to explain.

Laurie picked up her pencil and wrote in the margin, haltingly, in the way she wrote Spanish, each letter escorted by doubt. Then she covered the article with a menu and turned her face to the window. "Okay. Summary. From memory. Aloud. Dakota, time me."

"Sixty seconds. Go."

"The article is about a town where the water might be bad. According to the mayor, the water is safe. But, according to a residents' group, the water is not safe, and they want tests. The paper does not say who is right. The paper says what each side says. The reporter is not the referee. The reporter is the... the person at the door taking everyone's coats."

"That's your summary?" Dakota said. "That's a summary of the summary."

"It's what the article is. It's a machine for saying según. Somebody says a thing, the paper says that somebody said the thing. It's like a rule. A heuristic, basically. See según, hear a voice, not the reporter's."

Maggie raised her glass of tap water and studied it against the light with theatrical suspicion. "And suddenly every glass in this restaurant is a question."

"According to Maggie, this water is safe," Dakota intoned.

"According to Dakota, that joke was funny," Laurie said, and folded the newspaper along its original creases, careful now, as if the words might shift under her fingers when she wasn't watching. Monday felt less like a cliff and more like a long staircase she could actually see the bottom of, though she still couldn't say, out loud, whether she trusted the mayor, or the residents' group, or anything in Valencia except the grammar. Ms. Chukwu refilled their waters without being asked, set the pitcher down, and said, "On the house. According to me."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Mixing paints is subtractive: each pigment absorbs some wavelengths of light, so mixing many pigments together tends toward a dark, muddy color rather than white.
story:
The art shed at Camp Wanikan smelled of cedar shavings and turpentine, and by the second week Jaxon had claimed the corner table by the window as his own. He was painting a gift for his mother, who was recovering from surgery in a hospital room he imagined as beige and merciless, and he wanted the canvas to hold the exact color of the lake at seven in the evening, when the water went from blue to something brighter and stranger, a color he could see in his head but not, so far, on any brush.

He had started with blue and white. That had been fine, if ordinary. Then he wanted the green beneath the surface to show through, so he added green, and then a drop of yellow for the light, and then a little more blue because it had gone too yellow, and then, in a moment he would think about later with real embarrassment, a dot of red, because the lake at dusk had that faint warmth at the edges. He stirred. The paint on his palette knife turned the color of a puddle in a parking lot.

"That's brown," said Lena, who had been sitting across from him for an hour, sewing a wristband out of scavenged leather scraps. Lena wanted, more than anything this summer, to get moved up to the advanced craft rotation, which met at the kiln on the far side of camp, and the leather wristband was her audition piece for Ms. Popescu, who decided such things.

"It's lake-colored," Jaxon said, querulous even to himself, and he dipped the knife in and streaked the brown across the corner of the canvas where the bright color was supposed to live. It looked like mud. It looked like mud in a way that was almost impressive, a perfect and total mud.

He tried to rescue it. More white, more yellow, a reckless amount of orange. Each addition made it worse, and each worse version made him add more, and somewhere in the middle of that spiral he stopped and put the knife down because his hands were shaking, which felt ridiculous, and because the paint had begun to look the same no matter what he poured into it, a dark, dirty sameness, as though the colors were cancelling each other rather than combining.

Lena watched him from across the table, her needle paused. "You keep adding and it keeps getting darker," she said. "That's backwards, isn't it? Light mixes one way and paint mixes the other."

"It's subtractive," said Noemy, who had drifted over from the pottery wheel with clay to her elbows. She was the quiet one of the three of them, but she read physics books in her bunk after lights-out, and she said it simply, without a lecture in it: "Mixing paints is subtractive. Every pigment absorbs some wavelengths of light. So mixing a lot of pigments together goes toward a dark, muddy color, not white. You're not adding, you're taking away."

Jaxon looked at his palette, at the six little hills of paint he had folded into one another, and understood that he had been fighting the physics of light itself with a palette knife. He laughed, once, without much humor in it. His mother's hospital room floated back to him, and the lake color he could still see perfectly behind his eyes, and for a moment the whole project felt impossible, a gift made of mud for a woman who deserved something bright.

"Start over," Noemy said. "And don't mix everything. Mix two."

He scraped the palette clean, the paint curling off in brown ribbons that smelled faintly of linseed oil, and began again with just blue and white, no green, no red, no warmth at the edges. It came out cleaner than anything he had made all summer, a cool blue that was not quite the lake but was honest, and around its border he painted a thin band of pure yellow, unmixed, laid down in one unbroken stroke, so the two colors sat side by side and made the brightness between them that the paint itself could not.

Lena held up her finished wristband to the light. The stitching was uneven in one place and perfect everywhere else. She carried it across the shed to where Ms. Popescu was cataloging glazes, and Jaxon watched the teacher turn it over twice in her clay-dusted hands.

"The kiln group meets at four," Ms. Popescu said, and Lena walked back to the table very slowly, the way a person walks when they are trying not to run.

Jaxon turned back to his canvas. There was still one corner left, the brown corner, and he looked at it for a long moment, brush in hand. Then he painted the mud flat and even and left it there, a small dark square at the edge of all that blue and yellow, and signed his name in the bottom corner with a brush so thin it was almost a hair.

"For the record," he said, "the lake is still prettier."

"Obviously," said Noemy, and went back to her wheel.

activity: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
knowledge_domain: to apply a feminist or Marxist critical lens to a passage from a classic novel
fact: Virginia Woolf's A Room of One's Own, published in 1929, argues that a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction.
story:
Ms. Mori put the passage from the classic novel on the board, half a page describing a young woman whose beauty was her whole inheritance, and told them to read it twice before anyone spoke. Parker read it once and already felt the argument forming, the way he could usually feel an answer before he could say it. In margin notes he had been practicing all term, he wrote property, then wrote marriage as transaction, and underlined both.

"Marxist lens," he said when she called on him. "The woman is being exchanged. Her father converts her into social standing."

"Fine," said Ms. Mori. "Now apply the feminist lens to the same passage. Not a different passage. This one."

The two lenses kept sliding apart in his head. The Marxist reading made the woman an object of trade; the feminist reading, he thought, was supposed to make her a subject, but the passage gave her no interiority at all, only a face and a dowry. He said this badly and Calum, two seats over, laughed shortly.

"You're mad because she doesn't have thoughts," Calum said. "Maybe that's the point."

"Maybe you're the point," Leanne said, not looking up from her paper.

Ms. Mori moved on, but Parker copied the passage out by hand that evening at the library table by the window, where the radiator clanked and the light went orange by five. He wanted the essay to be right, and he could feel right slipping away from him the longer he looked. He tried to contextualize the novel, checking the year it was published, the class of its author, the audience it was written for, and each fact made the woman in the passage smaller, more surrounded.

Leanne dropped into the chair across from him with her own books. She had a battered paperback open, its spine cracked white, and she was annotating it in pencil with quick strokes.

"What is that," Parker said.

"A Room of One's Own. Virginia Woolf, 1929." She turned it toward him. "She argues a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction."

He wrote the title down. "That's why the reading list is like that, isn't it. Almost no women."

"I asked Ms. Mori that in September. She said make it a research question." Leanne took the paperback back. "It's not that the women weren't writing. Some were. It's that the list was made by people who didn't count them."

Parker sat with that. He had been treating the passage as a puzzle with a solution, one correct lens that would click over the lock, and the fact of Woolf's argument kept refusing to fit. If the woman in the novel had no money and no room, then she could not have written the novel, which meant the silence Parker kept bumping into was structural, not an accident of characterization. Both his lenses were saying something adjacent to this, but neither said it whole.

"It's not either," he said slowly. "It's both, but the feminist reading has to come first, because the Marxist one alone treats her like capital. She's not only capital. She's someone who couldn't even write her side of it."

"Congratulations," Leanne said. "You've discovered the silence in the text."

"That's smug."

"You're the one who underlined your own notes twice."

He looked down at his page, where property and marriage as transaction sat in his handwriting, already looking like someone else's certainty. He was honest enough with himself to admit he didn't know whether the synthesis held, whether putting the feminist lens first was a real position or just a nicer arrangement of things he'd been handed. He started drafting anyway, writing until the radiator stopped and the window went dark.

Calum found him at his locker the next morning. "You finished the essay?"

"Mostly."

"Ms. Mori will shred it if you hedge everything."

"Then she'll shred it." Parker shut his locker and held the essay against his chest. "Leanne's lending me the Woolf after break."

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Lynn Hunt's 1984 book Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution turned attention to symbols, language and festivals as sources for understanding the Revolution.
story:
Laurie sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with seven library books fanned around her like a hand of cards she did not know how to play. The assignment sheet, pinned under her ankle, read: "Trace how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800. Historiographical essay. Six pages." Ms. Huang had said the word historiography slowly, twice, as if tasting it, and then had smiled in a way that suggested the difficulty was the point.

The problem was not the Revolution itself. Laurie could recite the Terror, the Bastille, the committees of public safety; she had done that since tenth grade. The problem was that the books disagreed, and they disagreed not about facts but about what counted as facts. One author called the Revolution the birth of modern democracy; another called it a descent into ideological violence; a third seemed to think both versions were self-serving fictions. She flipped through them, stopped at a sentence about festivals and symbols, and felt the beginning of a question forming, small and cold, like a draft under a door.

She called Jasmine, who was good at arguing and bad at writing, an inverse Laurie found fascinating. "Okay," Jasmine said through the speaker, chewing something, "so pick a side. That's what an essay is, right? A side with footnotes."

"But what if the sides are the wrong thing to count?" Laurie looked at the postcard taped above her desk, bought last spring at the museum in the city: a reproduction of a revolutionary poster, a woman in a Phrygian cap trampling chains, and beneath her the single word LIBERTÉ. She had bought it because the colors were fierce, red and a strange hopeful blue. "When we were at the museum I stood in front of that poster for like ten minutes and I kept thinking, why is this here? It's not a document. It's decoration. Except what if it's not?" She could hear her own voice speeding up, the way it did when she was chasing something. "What if the picture is the evidence?"

"That's the weirdest sentence you've said all week, and last week you explained cicadas to me for forty minutes."

"Eshal would get it," Laurie said, and Jasmine laughed, because Eshal, who read everything and loved nothing more than a discarded footnote, absolutely would. Laurie hung up promising to send a draft, then pulled her laptop over and typed the poster's catalog number into the library database. An article came up first, then a chapter, then a citation she copied out by hand because it felt important enough to deserve her handwriting: Lynn Hunt, 1984, Politics, Culture, and Class in the French Revolution.

She read for two hours without noticing the time. Hunt, it turned out, had turned attention to symbols, language, festivals, exactly the things Laurie had been staring at on her wall, treating them as sources for understanding the Revolution rather than as wallpaper around the serious politics. A garrulous old textbook on the shelf beside her went on for pages about committees and constitutions and never once mentioned what the revolutionaries wore, sang, or put on their banners; another, older still, seemed designed to inculcate reverence for great men, its prose thick with a kind of mendacity by omission, as though the crowd in the street were simply an obstacle to the ambitions of the narrators' heroes. Laurie felt something shift, not a click exactly but a loosening, like a knot she had been picking at finally giving way.

She messaged Eshal. "Tell me if this makes sense. So the Marxists look at class. Then in 1984 Hunt says look at culture, symbols, festivals, language. And then the people after her argue with her, but on her terms, the terms she made. So the essay isn't me picking a side about the Revolution. It's me showing how the question itself changed."

Eshal replied with a thumbs up and then, thirty seconds later, a longer message: "Yes but be careful, my brother did something like this and his teacher said he never actually said what he thinks. You have to land somewhere." Laurie read that twice. Landing somewhere. She looked at the poster again, at the woman's bare foot on the broken chain, and admitted to the empty room that she did not entirely know where she stood: whether the turn to symbols had deepened history or merely decorated it, whether a festival could carry the same weight as a bread riot. She was honest enough with herself to write that uncertainty into the margin of her outline, a question mark shaped almost like a hook.

Her mother knocked and put a cup of tea on the desk without a word, the way she did during every exam season, and Laurie drank half of it cold. At one in the morning she typed her first real sentence, deleted it, typed it again with one clause added, and then leaned back and read it aloud to the woman on the wall. "By 1984, the questions historians asked had changed shape, and the shape was made of things like you." She laughed at herself, quietly, and kept typing.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: In Canadian federal elections, an eligible voter who is not on the voters list can register at their assigned polling place on election day.
story:
Savannah had told everyone she was ready. She had told Sonya twice on the walk over, once at the door of the community hall, and once more in the line that snaked between the folding tables, that she had done her research, that she knew exactly which candidate she was marking her ballot for, and this was mostly true, except for the part where she had never actually registered to vote and was certain, in the way she was certain about things she hadn't checked, that this meant she would be turned away.

"I studied the platforms," she said to Sonya, who was juggling her wallet, her keys, and a muffin with the top bitten off. "All of them. Even the ones with no chance. I made a spreadsheet."

"You made a spreadsheet," Kayla said, falling into line behind them with rain still beaded on her jacket. "Savannah. It's one X."

"It's not one X, it's a decision." Savannah held her ID against her chest like a shield, though she could not have said against what. The hall smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee, and along the far wall a table of seniors ladled soup into bowls for the after-voting crowd, an act of such steady, unannounced kindness that she felt briefly ashamed of her spreadsheet.

When her turn came, the poll worker was Mr. Costa, who had taught her Grade Nine geography and still wore the same cardigan, the cuffs gone soft. He found her name nowhere in the binder, and Savannah felt her certainty arrive exactly on schedule: she had missed the deadline, she had ruined it, eighteen years old and already disqualified by her own carelessness. She began composing the text to Sonya, who had sailed through two tables over and was waiting by the ballot box with an expression of effusive, unbearable sympathy from across the room.

"You're not on the list," Mr. Costa said, and turned the binder toward her as if inviting her to be disappointed alongside him.

"I know," Savannah said. "I never registered. I thought you had to do it ahead of time."

"In a Canadian federal election, if you're eligible and you're not on the voters list, you can register right here, at your polling place, on election day."

She stared at him. "Today? Now?"

"That's the idea." He slid a form across the table and uncapped a pen. "ID with your address?"

She produced her driver's licence, her care card, and, for reasons she declined to verbalize, a library card, and Mr. Costa took only the first one and checked the second against a laminated sheet. Her hands were less steady than she would have reported them. Somewhere behind her, a man with a cane asked whether there was a chair he could use while he waited, and the woman at the soup table carried one out to him without a word, setting it down at the end of the line so he wouldn't have to ask twice.

While she printed her name and address in the small boxes, Savannah considered that her spreadsheet, for all its tabs and colour coding, had not contained a single column for how to actually vote, and that her confidence had been a kind of asceticism, really, a discipline of preparation so severe it had starved out the ordinary questions. Kayla, who had claimed to know nothing, had known to bring her hydro bill. Sonya, who studied only when she felt like it, had known to check her registration card in the junk drawer. Savannah had known the platforms and not the door.

The booth was a cardboard screen on a metal frame, and inside it the pencil was tied to a string. Her candidate's name was printed in the third row down. She held the pencil over the circle and found that the certainty she had carried all morning had thinned, not into doubt exactly, but into something quieter: a decision she could still defend, made by a person who now knew slightly less about herself than she'd thought, and was, for the first time that day, being honest about it. She made her X. She folded the paper along its creases and carried it to the box, where Sonya was waiting, and where Kayla had saved her a place at the soup table.

"Well?" Sonya said. "Feel different?"

Savannah slid her ballot into the slot and listened for the soft sound it made landing.

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: In Peter Wason's 1966 selection task, people must pick which cards to turn over to test an if-then rule; in his study, fewer than 10 percent chose the correct cards in the abstract version.
story:
The library had a study room you could requisition for two hours at a time, and Nathan had signed out Room C every Thursday since September, which was why it stung when he found Emrik already inside, boots on the second chair, spreading a psychology textbook across the table like he owned the walls.

"Room's mine," Nathan said.

"Checked the sheet. Nobody booked it." Emrik slid a page toward him, a photocopy with four rectangles drawn on it. "Ms. Sharma left these at the desk. She said try it before tomorrow."

Farhan arrived with two vending machine cookies and dropped into the third chair, already chewing. Each card had one face showing: a vowel, D, the number seven, the number four. The rule, printed at the top, said that if a card has a vowel on one side, then it has an even number on the other. "Which cards do you turn over to test it," Farhan read aloud, "and only those cards."

"A and seven," Emrik said, tapping without hesitation. "You check the vowel, and you check the seven, because seven's odd, so if it's hiding a vowel the rule's dead."

Nathan looked at the page. The reasoning felt clean, the way a locker slams shut. "That makes sense," he said, and reached for a cookie.

Farhan turned his cookie over in his fingers, slow, as if the chocolate chips might spell something. "Wait. Turn over the four. If the four has a vowel behind it."

"Then nothing happens," Emrik said. "The rule only says vowels get even numbers. It doesn't say even numbers get vowels." He said it in the tone he used when he'd already decided the conversation was beneath him, the tone their whole grade called his locker-room voice.

Nathan wrote the rule at the top of his notes anyway, if vowel, then even, and underneath it began to flip it, not the cards but the sentence itself. If not even, then not vowel. Those seemed to say the same thing in opposite clothes. Which meant the seven was the one to watch, sure, but so was the A, and only those two, and nothing about the four mattered at all. He said so, and Emrik shrugged like they'd agreed all along, which they had not.

Ms. Sharma passed the open door with a cart of returns, paused, and looked over Farhan's shoulder. "How are my logicians?" Her voice had a querulous edge on Thursdays, worn thin by sixth period. "Don't tell me. You chose the A and the seven."

"Obviously," Emrik said.

"Peter Wason ran this task in 1966," she said, pulling a stray pencil from the photocopy. "In the abstract version, fewer than ten percent of people picked the correct cards." She tapped the A, then the seven, then left, wheeling the cart toward the front desk where a boy was trying to argue his way out of a two-dollar fine, saying the word insolvency with total confidence and no meaning, as if the library were a bank about to fail him.

Farhan laughed so hard a crumb went up his nose. "So we're the ninety percent. Emrik, you're a statistic."

"I said A and seven," Emrik said, but he said it toward the window.

"You said A and seven because it made sense," Nathan said. "I said it because you said it." He wrote that down too, because it was the kind of thing he'd want to remember later, when the wanting to be right started feeling like hunger. The room went quiet except for the heating vent and the distant cashier telling the insolvency boy that a fine was not a debt to society.

"Here's the thing, though," Nathan went on, and he turned the paper so both of them could see it. "Checking the seven, that's looking for the rule to fail. Checking the A, that's looking for it to hold. You need both, but the failing one is the one everybody skips, because nobody wants to hunt for their own side being wrong." He paused. "Maybe. I might be stretching it."

"You're always stretching it," Emrik said, but without the locker-room voice this time. He took out a pen and drew a fifth card, blank, and stared at it. "So tomorrow, when she does it with the class."

"We say nothing," Farhan said. "We watch them all pick A and four."

"Not four," Nathan said. "A and four is the trap. It'll be A and seven half the time and A and four the rest." He wasn't sure that was true, and he said so, and Emrik said that was the most honest thing Nathan had produced all year.

They stayed past the hour mark, Farhan inventing card games with worse and worse rules, Emrik defending each one as testable, Nathan keeping the list. When the desk lamp flickered, they packed up, and at the door Emrik tore off the blank fifth card, folded it in half, and set it back on the table.

"For the next person," he said.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Sociologist Mark Granovetter's 1973 paper 'The Strength of Weak Ties' found that people often learned of new jobs through acquaintances rather than close friends.
story:
The house had no furniture in it yet, only their footsteps, and every sound Brianna made came back to her off the bare walls like someone else walking in another room. She carried a box marked DESK up the stairs, set it down in the room with the good window, and called Lyric because that was what she did when something happened, good or bad or nothing at all.

"You're breathing into an empty house," Lyric said. "That's so bleak. It sounds like a haunted podcast."

"It has a window seat," Brianna said. "You would love the window seat."

"I'm sure I would, if I lived three hundred miles away from it." There was a rustle on the other end, Lyric flopping onto her bed the way she always did, phone held above her face. "Mustafa says hi. He's here, obviously. It's Tuesday."

Tuesday was dumplings at the place near school, the table by the window, the three of them arguing about whether the dumplings were actually good or just familiar. Brianna sat down on the floor because there was nowhere else to sit, and she could almost feel the cracked vinyl of the booth through the phone.

Downstairs her mother was arguing with the movers about the piano, which had belonged to Brianna's grandmother and which none of them could really play. "It underwrites the whole living room," her mother kept saying, which was not a word anyone in the family used correctly, and which the movers ignored entirely. Brianna hung up before Lyric could ask her what she was going to do out here, because she didn't know, and she didn't want Lyric to hear the pause where the answer should have been.

The next afternoon she walked the neighborhood because there was nothing else to do, and because the empty house made her feel atavistic, like some early mammal prowling the edge of new territory. Two streets over, a woman was wrestling a folding sign out onto the sidewalk in front of a café. Brianna had met her exactly twice: once at the closing, where the woman had said the previous owners never fixed anything, and once yesterday, when she'd waved from her porch while Brianna's father swore at the mailbox. The café woman saw her and stopped struggling with the sign long enough to look at her properly.

"You're the piano people," she said. "Do you want a job? I need someone Saturdays and two afternoons. My last girl went off to college and gave me four days' notice, which, honestly, I respect."

"Me?" said Brianna, who had applied to nothing, who had planned to apply to everything, who had a whole spreadsheet of places that had not yet been contacted.

"You're ambulatory and you made eye contact," the woman said. "That puts you in the top phylum of job applicants. Can you wash dishes without narrating your feelings about it? The last one narrated."

Brianna texted Lyric from the café's back step: got a job. how. i have applied to ZERO places. Lyric replied with a row of exclamation points and then, three minutes later, a screenshot from something called "The Strength of Weak Ties," a 1973 paper by a sociologist named Mark Granovetter. Her older sister was reading it for a class. Brianna read the screenshot twice. People often learned of new jobs through acquaintances rather than close friends. She read it a third time, sitting on the warm concrete with someone's espresso cup balanced on her knee.

"So basically my close friends are useless," she said to Mustafa that night, three-way call, Lyric's phone propped against the salt shaker at the dumpling place so the two of them could see the table without her. "The paper says it's the weak ties. I got a job from a woman I've met twice, and you two have gotten me nothing."

"We got you a personality," Mustafa said. "Take that up with Granovetter."

"It's not that they're useless," Lyric said, in the voice she used when she was right and being generous about it. "It's that close friends know the same things you know. It's the people at the edges who have the stuff you don't." Then, quieter, "Are you going to have edges there? People at them, I mean."

Brianna said she would, and it came out more certain than she felt. Because here was the thing she couldn't say on the call: the weak ties had worked, exactly like the paper said, and it had still felt like luck, like a door opening onto a room she hadn't earned. She had wanted to do it properly, spreadsheet and all, and instead a woman who knew her only as "the piano people" had handed her Saturdays. Maybe the edges were where things happened, or maybe she was a girl who happened to be standing on a sidewalk. She held both of those ideas at once and could not get them to fit together, and she thought maybe that was allowed.

On Saturday she worked her first shift, and the espresso machine hissed, and a boy from the high school she would start on Monday came in and ordered something complicated, and the café woman said, "That's Brianna, she's new," and the boy said, "Oh yeah? I'm new too, sort of," and neither of them looked away.

That night Brianna dragged a beanbag up to the room with the good window and texted Lyric a photo of the window seat with her in it, and Lyric texted back the dumpling table, empty, with a single sad fork laid across it, and the caption: table for one, you absolute traitor. Brianna laughed, then didn't, then laughed again, and out past the glass the unfamiliar street held its one streetlight like it was waiting to see what she'd do about it.
